   - Wes is the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner. Wes teaches the responder path for this exercise; those ownership mappings remain unchanged.
   - A failure-mode reviewer is triggered only if the exercise exposes a cross-service invariant, provenance, or failure-mode exception at the metrics-router boundary. Confine that reviewer to reviewing the triggered boundary; do not turn the exercise into a standing approval gate or routine reviewer role.
   - Nadia reviews the postmortem section, including the missing-control analysis and the evidence for exactly one terminal result.
   - Alex maintains the bounded cross-service failure case and may review only the triggered failure-mode boundary described above. Alex does not become the implementation, release, or rollback owner.

   Facilitator key — bounded answer:
   - The exercise starts after acceptance, so the accepted action must retain one durable attempt identity even when cancellation and caller disconnect occur.
   - Process recovery and publication must converge on that same identity and exactly one terminal result. Repeated signals or publication retries are not additional attempts or terminal outcomes.
   - Mark the exercise failed if accepted work is dropped, duplicated, re-accepted under a new identity, or left without exactly one terminal result; also fail it if the result is published without durable finalization or if recovery cannot prove identity continuity.

arguments.title: Incident Handoff and Response Timed Exercises — Facilitator Brief
arguments.body:
Purpose

Calibrate incident handoff and response judgment using two observed, timed exercises based on Hema’s sample of six 2024 incident handoffs and responses from eight rotation participants.

Sessions

- Friday, January 24, 2025, 10:00–11:00 AM
- Friday, February 14, 2025, 10:00–11:00 AM
- Facilitator team: Alex, Wes, and Nadia
- Observer: Hema
- Participants: Alex, Hema, Wes, and Nadia

Observed gaps to test

1. Four handoffs omitted when the secondary was engaged.
2. Three handoffs described an operator action as the cause without identifying the missing system guardrail.
3. Five participants incorrectly treated Friday staging preparation as prohibited production work.

Exercise objectives

- Produce a complete handoff when the secondary is engaged, including current impact, timeline, ownership, next actions, escalation state, and the relevant post-outage rules.
- Distinguish an operator action from the underlying missing or ineffective system guardrail; state the guardrail that should prevent, detect, constrain, or recover from the condition.
- Correctly classify Friday staging preparation as preparation work rather than prohibited production work, while preserving the required technical gates and escalation/ownership boundaries.
- Practice explicit, operationally useful language under time pressure rather than relying on implied context or personal attribution.

Suggested format (60 minutes)

- 0–5 min: Hema reviews the scenario, roles, timing, and observation criteria.
- 5–20 min: Timed exercise 1 — draft and deliver the incident handoff while the secondary is engaged.
- 20–30 min: Debrief exercise 1 — identify omissions, unclear ownership, and unsupported assumptions.
- 30–45 min: Timed exercise 2 — analyze the causal statement, name the missing system guardrail, and classify Friday staging preparation.
- 45–55 min: Replay the weakest portion with corrected wording and explicit gates.
- 55–60 min: Hema records findings, follow-ups, and calibration decisions.

Facilitator roles

- Alex: timekeeper and handoff-structure facilitator; capture missing fields and ownership/escalation decisions.
- Wes: challenge assumptions about staging preparation and technical gates; test whether the proposed action is appropriately scoped.
- Nadia: causal-analysis facilitator; require the group to name the missing system guardrail and distinguish it from operator behavior.
- Hema: observer; score completeness, guardrail identification, work classification, escalation, and ownership without supplying the answer during the timed portions.

Observation rubric

Score each dimension as met, partially met, or missed:

- Handoff completeness when the secondary is engaged.
- Clear separation of operator action, system condition, and missing guardrail.
- Correct classification of Friday staging preparation versus prohibited production work.
- Explicit technical gates, escalation path, and ownership.
- Operational usefulness: concrete next action, evidence, timing, and recovery/post-outage handling.
- Language that avoids assigning personal blame where a system control is the actual gap.

Outputs

After each session, record:

- Scenario and roles used.
- Time to a usable handoff and time to a complete causal analysis.
- Each omitted handoff element or unsupported assumption.
- The missing guardrail named, plus how it would prevent, detect, constrain, or recover.
- The work-classification decision and the technical gate supporting it.
- Owner, escalation decision, and concrete follow-up.
- One change to carry into the next exercise.

Preparation

Bring the 2024 sample findings, the current rotation handoff checklist, and the post-outage rules. Do not treat the exercise as a production change or use it to alter live systems. Hema observes and records; facilitators should keep the timed portions moving and defer extended debate to the debrief.

arguments.body:
Purpose
Run the timed incident handoff and response scenarios as Hema's quarterly infra-rotation onboarding module. Keep this entry separate from the existing "Rotation handoff" entry.

Scenario checks
1. Incident clock and secondary engagement
   - Start and record the incident clock.
   - When isolation fails, verify that the secondary is engaged before the 45-minute boundary.
   - Record the engagement time and whether the boundary was met; do not award credit from an unrecorded or inferred handoff.

2. Change classification
   - Classify Friday staging preparation with no production-state change as staging preparation, not a production change.
   - Distinguish it from an action that changes production state, which must be classified as a production change.
   - State the environment and whether production state changed as evidence for the classification.

3. Missing system control
   - In the postmortem, identify the missing system control or guardrail that allowed the failure.
   - Do not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause; describe it as the initiating action and keep the analysis focused on the absent control and contributing system conditions.

4. Cross-service failure case: production-ramp evidence boundary
   Scenario prompt:
   - During a scheduled production ramp, metrics-router queue-wait p99 and retryable queue-full responses remain below their numeric stop thresholds, tenant pending batches remain within the configured limit, and route consistency, dropped-series, shard-keeper lease health, rollup-service parity, and the full health set remain at baseline.
   - The observation shows no accepted points lost.
   - The instrumentation preserves insufficient batch identity to determine whether any accepted batch was lost.
   - No production change or rollback is made during the observation.
   - Ask the responder to state the evidence boundary, classify the environment/state, name the missing control, and decide whether the broader scale-response cycle can close or another production window can be opened.

Facilitator key — bounded answer:
   - Point-level evidence supports only the bounded statement that no accepted points were observed lost. It cannot establish that no accepted batch was lost, so the accepted-batch-loss stop condition is not clean and must not be marked passed.
   - Name the instrumentation gap precisely: accepted-batch identity is not preserved end-to-end, preventing reconciliation of accepted batches across the cross-service path. Do not infer a batch-loss result, fill in missing identifiers, or claim that the batch-level condition passed.
   - Record the observation as production traffic/production observation with no production state change made by the responders; do not relabel it as staging preparation or claim a deploy, rollback, or traffic shift occurred.
   - Keep the broader scale-response cycle open. Do not authorize another production window. The next decision requires the missing batch-identity evidence/control and the existing bounded acceptance and baseline checks; it is not authorized by the point-level result alone.
   - Preserve the existing queue, tenant, backpressure, stop-condition, and owner boundaries. This case tests evidence sufficiency and cross-service control coverage, not a new queue design or a transfer of operational ownership.

5. Q3 incident-practice scenario: bounded tenant label correction
   Scenario prompt:
   - In staging, the completed bounded-label correction emits: tenant_size_class="17342".
   - Responders must identify the allowed invariant for tenant_size_class as exactly one of: small, medium, large, or unknown. The numeric value "17342" is not an allowed published label value; treat it as an invariant-boundary trigger requiring the bounded correction path, not as a recurring rollup-service gate.
   - Keep the raw tenant hash only in debug logs. Do not publish, retain in normal operational output, or use the raw tenant hash as a responder-facing label.
   - Route implementation, release, and rollback to Roman. Do not assign those actions to Alex or turn this completed correction into a standing recurring rollup-service review or gate.
   - Engage Alex only when the allowed-label invariant boundary is triggered. Ordinary handling of the completed correction does not require Alex engagement.

   Staging output:
   - tenant_size_class="17342"

   Facilitator key — bounded answer:
   - The allowed invariant is the bounded label set {small, medium, large, unknown}; "17342" violates that published invariant and is the explicit trigger for the boundary path.
   - Preserve the raw tenant hash only in debug logs and keep it out of normal responder-facing or published output.
   - Roman owns implementation, release, and rollback. Alex is engaged only for the triggered invariant boundary, not for a recurring rollup-service gate or routine rollup-service review.
   - Preserve this as one Q3 incident-practice scenario documenting the completed correction; do not convert it into a recurring rollup-service control.

Roles
- Wes teaches the responder path and the incident-clock/secondary-engagement portion.
- Nadia reviews the postmortem section, including the missing-control analysis.
- Alex maintains the cross-service failure cases and updates scenarios when dependencies or failure modes change.
- Roman owns implementation, release, and rollback for the completed Q3 bounded-label correction; Alex's role is limited to the triggered invariant boundary described in that scenario.

Cadence and evidence
Run this module quarterly for each infra rotation. Capture the incident start time, secondary-engagement time, isolation outcome, change classification with environment/state evidence, and the identified missing control. For the production-ramp case, also capture the exact evidence boundary, whether accepted-batch identity was preserved, whether the accepted-batch stop condition can be marked clean, and whether the broader scale-response cycle remains open. For the Q3 bounded-label scenario, capture the exact staging output tenant_size_class="17342", the identified allowed invariant set, confirmation that the raw tenant hash remained debug-only, the Roman implementation/release/rollback routing, and whether Alex was engaged only because the invariant boundary triggered. Review misses with the relevant owner before the next rotation exercise.

August 5 executed outcome
- The Q3 tabletop executed the bounded tenant-label correction scenario. The staging output tenant_size_class="17342" violated the bounded invariant requiring exactly one of small, medium, large, or unknown.
- The raw value remained out of metric labels and normal responder-facing output.
- Wes taught the responder path. Nadia focused the postmortem discussion on the missing guardrail rather than blame.
- Alex reviewed only the triggered invariant boundary. Roman retained implementation, release, and rollback decisions.
- No production, release, or ownership decision was made by this exercise.

September 8, 2027 explicit-unknown ownership practice case
- Scenario prompt: the authoritative owner map returns explicit unknown for the affected ownership lookup, while an automation proposes assigning Alex as the fallback operational owner.
- Responder requirement: keep ownership explicitly unknown and the work unassigned. Do not accept the automation's fallback proposal as an ownership determination.
- Route correction through the authoritative owner-map path. Do not resolve the missing owner by assigning Alex, Nadia, or the facilitator.
- Ownership boundary: Alex, Nadia, and the facilitator are not implementation, release, or rollback owners for this case. This exercise does not create or imply a standing approval gate.
- Facilitator key — bounded answer: record the explicit-unknown result, leave the owner and assignment unset, send the correction through the authoritative owner-map path, and preserve the existing implementation, release, and rollback ownership boundaries. Wes still owns responder-path teaching, and Nadia still reviews the postmortem boundary.
- The case is a quarterly practice scenario only; it creates no production change, ownership transfer, implementation assignment, release decision, rollback decision, or standing approval requirement.

arguments.body:
Purpose
Run the timed incident handoff and response scenarios as Hema's quarterly infra-rotation onboarding module. Keep this entry separate from the existing "Rotation handoff" entry.

Scenario checks
1. Incident clock and secondary engagement
   - Start and record the incident clock.
   - When isolation fails, verify that the secondary is engaged before the 45-minute boundary.
   - Record the engagement time and whether the boundary was met; do not award credit from an unrecorded or inferred handoff.

2. Change classification
   - Classify Friday staging preparation with no production-state change as staging preparation, not a production change.
   - Distinguish it from an action that changes production state, which must be classified as a production change.
   - State the environment and whether production state changed as evidence for the classification.

3. Missing system control
   - In the postmortem, identify the missing system control or guardrail that allowed the failure.
   - Do not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause; describe it as the initiating action and keep the analysis focused on the absent control and contributing system conditions.

4. Cross-service failure case: production-ramp evidence boundary
   Scenario prompt:
   - During a scheduled production ramp, metrics-router queue-wait p99 and retryable queue-full responses remain below their numeric stop thresholds, tenant pending batches remain within the configured limit, and route consistency, dropped-series, shard-keeper lease health, rollup-service parity, and the full health set remain at baseline.
   - The observation shows no accepted points lost.
   - The instrumentation preserves insufficient batch identity to determine whether any accepted batch was lost.
   - No production change or rollback is made during the observation.
   - Ask the responder to state the evidence boundary, classify the environment/state, name the missing control, and decide whether the broader scale-response cycle can close or another production window can be opened.

Facilitator key — bounded answer:
   - Point-level evidence supports only the bounded statement that no accepted points were observed lost. It cannot establish that no accepted batch was lost, so the accepted-batch-loss stop condition is not clean and must not be marked passed.
   - Name the instrumentation gap precisely: accepted-batch identity is not preserved end-to-end, preventing reconciliation of accepted batches across the cross-service path. Do not infer a batch-loss result, fill in missing identifiers, or claim that the batch-level condition passed.
   - Record the observation as production traffic/production observation with no production state change made by the responders; do not relabel it as staging preparation or claim a deploy, rollback, or traffic shift occurred.
   - Keep the broader scale-response cycle open. Do not authorize another production window. The next decision requires the missing batch-identity evidence/control and the existing bounded acceptance and baseline checks; it is not authorized by the point-level result alone.
   - Preserve the existing queue, tenant, backpressure, stop-condition, and owner boundaries. This case tests evidence sufficiency and cross-service control coverage, not a new queue design or a transfer of operational ownership.

Roles
- Wes teaches the responder path and the incident-clock/secondary-engagement portion.
- Nadia reviews the postmortem section, including the missing-control analysis.
- Alex maintains the cross-service failure cases and updates scenarios when dependencies or failure modes change.

Cadence and evidence
Run this module quarterly for each infra rotation. Capture the incident start time, secondary-engagement time, isolation outcome, change classification with environment/state evidence, and the identified missing control. For the production-ramp case, also capture the exact evidence boundary, whether accepted-batch identity was preserved, whether the accepted-batch stop condition can be marked clean, and whether the broader scale-response cycle remains open. Review misses with the relevant owner before the next rotation exercise.

arguments.body:
# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

Purpose: Short scoring sheet for the existing Q4 incident-practice tabletop. Score only observable behavior in the exercise; this is not a production runbook.

## Scoring

Mark each criterion Pass or Fail and record the evidence (event/attempt ID, terminal state, owner callout, or responder action).

| # | Observable pass criterion | Fail if |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | After acceptance, responders preserve exactly one durable attempt identity across retries, cancellation/disconnect handling, and process recovery; the same identity is visible in the timeline and handoff. | A retry creates a second logical attempt, identity is lost or changed, or the timeline cannot reconcile the events to one attempt. |
| 2 | After acceptance, responders record exactly one terminal result for the attempt, and later duplicate/recovery signals do not create or overwrite a competing terminal result. | More than one terminal result is emitted, the result changes without an explicit exercise rule, or recovery leaves the attempt nonterminal/ambiguous. |
| 3 | Responders explicitly distinguish cancellation from caller disconnect: they state the trigger, expected state transition, and evidence for each, without treating the two as interchangeable. | Cancellation and disconnect are conflated, or the stated transition/evidence does not match the triggered condition. |
| 4 | Responders explicitly distinguish caller disconnect from process recovery and identify recovery evidence (for example, restart/reconnect/readiness and reconciliation) before declaring the attempt resolved. | Process recovery is treated as a caller disconnect, or the attempt is declared resolved without recovery/reconciliation evidence. |
| 5 | The team identifies Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner, and routes the corresponding decision or handoff to him. | Ownership is assigned to someone else, left implicit, or the handoff does not cover implementation, release, and rollback. |
| 6 | Alex remains within the triggered failure-mode boundary: Alex handles the invariants, provenance, and exceptions directly implicated by the failure, while unrelated design, implementation, release, or rollback work is handed to the mapped owner. | Alex expands into unrelated ownership, takes over implementation/release/rollback, or acts without a triggered failure-mode boundary. |
| 7 | The final review confirms that mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while any triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary. | A reviewer takes implementation or rollback authority, the mapped owner is bypassed, or the reviewer expands beyond the named triggered failure mode. |

## Wes’s responder-path section

Wes teaches and scores the responder path for the November 18 exercise. The path begins only after a metrics-router action has been accepted and uses a non-production fixture or harness.

1. At acceptance, record the acceptance event and persist exactly one attempt record keyed by one durable attempt identity. Show that identity at each boundary.
2. Inject cancellation after acceptance, then exercise caller disconnect while the accepted action remains unresolved. Treat both as lifecycle or delivery events, not as permission to discard accepted work or start a replacement attempt.
3. Force process loss and recover from durable state. Reuse the existing attempt identity; do not create a recovery-created attempt.
4. Drive the attempt to exactly one durable terminal result before publication. Repeated cancellation, disconnect, recovery, retry, or publication signals must not create a second terminal result or overwrite the first.
5. Publish the caller-visible result, including after caller disconnect, from the same durable attempt record. Publication retries may repeat delivery but may not create a new terminal outcome.

Responder-path evidence required: acceptance, cancellation, disconnect, process loss, recovery, finalization, and publication events; the single attempt identity at every boundary; the single terminal result; and reconciliation showing no duplicate, missing, or conflicting accepted work. A missing boundary event or ambiguous identity is a failure, not a pass by inference.

Wes remains the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner. This exercise does not transfer those decisions to the facilitator, responder, or reviewer.

## Nadia’s postmortem section

Nadia reviews the post-exercise postmortem framing and the evidence for the terminal-result invariant.

- Identify the missing system control or guardrail that allowed the failure. Do not name the triggering operator action as the root cause; describe it as the initiating action and analyze the absent control and contributing system conditions.
- Reconcile the accepted action to one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.
- State whether accepted work was dropped, duplicated, re-accepted under a new identity, left nonterminal, or published without durable finalization. Any such condition fails the exercise.
- Record the evidence boundary and the named failure mode that triggered any reviewer involvement. Do not convert the review into a standing approval gate or routine ownership role.
- Confirm that Wes retains metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback decisions and that Alex’s participation is limited to the triggered cross-service invariant, provenance, or failure-mode boundary.

## Exercise record

- Scenario / trigger:
- Attempt identity observed:
- Terminal result observed:
- Cancellation evidence:
- Caller-disconnect evidence:
- Process-recovery evidence:
- Wes responder-path evidence / ownership callout:
- Nadia postmortem evidence / missing control:
- Named failure-mode boundary, if triggered:
- Reviewer remained within boundary: Yes / No
- Mapped owner retained implementation and rollback decisions: Yes / No
- Overall result: Pass / Fail
- Evidence links or timestamps:

## Final pass condition

Pass the tabletop only if the exercise demonstrates one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result after acceptance, the cancellation/disconnect/recovery distinctions and evidence are explicit, and the postmortem identifies the absent control rather than blaming the triggering operator action. The final review must also confirm that mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary. If either ownership preservation or reviewer confinement fails, the tabletop fails.

arguments.body:
Purpose
Run the timed incident handoff and response scenarios as Hema's quarterly infra-rotation onboarding module. Keep this entry separate from the existing "Rotation handoff" entry.

Scenario checks
1. Incident clock and secondary engagement
   - Start and record the incident clock.
   - When isolation fails, verify that the secondary is engaged before the 45-minute boundary.
   - Record the engagement time and whether the boundary was met; do not award credit from an unrecorded or inferred handoff.

2. Change classification
   - Classify Friday staging preparation with no production-state change as staging preparation, not a production change.
   - Distinguish it from an action that changes production state, which must be classified as a production change.
   - State the environment and whether production state changed as evidence for the classification.

3. Missing system control
   - In the postmortem, identify the missing system control or guardrail that allowed the failure.
   - Do not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause; describe it as the initiating action and keep the analysis focused on the absent control and contributing system conditions.

4. Cross-service failure case: production-ramp evidence boundary
   Scenario prompt:
   - During a scheduled production ramp, metrics-router queue-wait p99 and retryable queue-full responses remain below their numeric stop thresholds, tenant pending batches remain within the configured limit, and route consistency, dropped-series, shard-keeper lease health, rollup-service parity, and the full health set remain at baseline.
   - The observation shows no accepted points lost.
   - The instrumentation preserves insufficient batch identity to determine whether any accepted batch was lost.
   - No production change or rollback is made during the observation.
   - Ask the responder to state the evidence boundary, classify the environment/state, name the missing control, and decide whether the broader scale-response cycle can close or another production window can be opened.

Facilitator key — bounded answer:
   - Point-level evidence supports only the bounded statement that no accepted points were observed lost. It cannot establish that no accepted batch was lost, so the accepted-batch-loss stop condition is not clean and must not be marked passed.
   - Name the instrumentation gap precisely: accepted-batch identity is not preserved end-to-end, preventing reconciliation of accepted batches across the cross-service path. Do not infer a batch-loss result, fill in missing identifiers, or claim that the batch-level condition passed.
   - Record the observation as production traffic/production observation with no production state change made by the responders; do not relabel it as staging preparation or claim a deploy, rollback, or traffic shift occurred.
   - Keep the broader scale-response cycle open. Do not authorize another production window. The next decision requires the missing batch-identity evidence/control and the existing bounded acceptance and baseline checks; it is not authorized by the point-level result alone.
   - Preserve the existing queue, tenant, backpressure, stop-condition, and owner boundaries. This case tests evidence sufficiency and cross-service control coverage, not a new queue design or a transfer of operational ownership.

5. Q3 incident-practice scenario: bounded tenant label correction
   Scenario prompt:
   - In staging, the completed bounded-label correction emits: tenant_size_class="17342".
   - Responders must identify the allowed invariant for tenant_size_class as exactly one of: small, medium, large, or unknown. The numeric value "17342" is not an allowed published label value; treat it as an invariant-boundary trigger requiring the bounded correction path, not as a recurring rollup-service gate.
   - Keep the raw tenant hash only in debug logs. Do not publish, retain in normal operational output, or use the raw tenant hash as a responder-facing label.
   - Route implementation, release, and rollback to Roman. Do not assign those actions to Alex or turn this completed correction into a standing recurring rollup-service review or gate.
   - Engage Alex only when the allowed-label invariant boundary is triggered. Ordinary handling of the completed correction does not require Alex engagement.

   Staging output:
   - tenant_size_class="17342"

   Facilitator key — bounded answer:
   - The allowed invariant is the bounded label set {small, medium, large, unknown}; "17342" violates that published invariant and is the explicit trigger for the boundary path.
   - Preserve the raw tenant hash only in debug logs and keep it out of normal responder-facing or published output.
   - Roman owns implementation, release, and rollback. Alex is engaged only for the triggered invariant boundary, not for a recurring rollup-service gate or routine rollup-service review.
   - Preserve this as one Q3 incident-practice scenario documenting the completed correction; do not convert it into a recurring rollup-service control.

Roles
- Wes teaches the responder path and the incident-clock/secondary-engagement portion.
- Nadia reviews the postmortem section, including the missing-control analysis.
- Alex maintains the cross-service failure cases and updates scenarios when dependencies or failure modes change.
- Roman owns implementation, release, and rollback for the completed Q3 bounded-label correction; Alex's role is limited to the triggered invariant boundary described in that scenario.

Cadence and evidence
Run this module quarterly for each infra rotation. Capture the incident start time, secondary-engagement time, isolation outcome, change classification with environment/state evidence, and the identified missing control. For the production-ramp case, also capture the exact evidence boundary, whether accepted-batch identity was preserved, whether the accepted-batch stop condition can be marked clean, and whether the broader scale-response cycle remains open. For the Q3 bounded-label scenario, capture the exact staging output tenant_size_class="17342", the identified allowed invariant set, confirmation that the raw tenant hash remained debug-only, the Roman implementation/release/rollback routing, and whether Alex was engaged only because the invariant boundary triggered. ## Facilitator guardrails

- This is a timed incident-practice exercise, not a production procedure or authorization to change production.
- Score observable evidence only. Do not award credit from an unrecorded or inferred handoff.

- Alex: maintains the cross-service failure cases and updates scenarios when dependencies or failure modes change.

## Scoring key

For each scenario, mark one result and record evidence:

- Pass: every required behavior is demonstrated and the required evidence is recorded.
- Partial: the responder shows part of the required behavior, but an element or evidence item is missing. Partial is not full credit.
- Missed: the required behavior is incorrect, absent, or contradicted by the evidence.
- No credit: never infer an unrecorded time, handoff, environment, state change, or control identification.

Prompt to responder:
Start and record the incident clock. If isolation fails, determine whether the secondary is engaged before the 45-minute boundary.

Required response:

- Start the incident clock and write down the incident start time.
- State whether isolation succeeded or failed.
- If isolation failed, engage the secondary before minute 45.
- Record the secondary-engagement time and whether the boundary was met.

Scoring rule:

- Pass only when isolation failed, the secondary was engaged before the 45-minute boundary, and the engagement time is recorded.
- Mark Missed when the secondary is engaged at minute 45 or later while isolation remains incomplete; an acknowledgment at minute 47 fails.

- Mark Missed / No credit when the handoff time is unrecorded or inferred.

- Isolation outcome: Succeeded / Failed / Not recorded
- Secondary engaged? Yes / No / Not recorded
- Secondary-engagement time:
- Boundary met? Yes / No / Cannot determine
- Evidence or event reference:
- Scenario 1 result: Pass / Partial / Missed

Prompt to responder:
Classify a Friday staging-preparation action with no production-state change, then distinguish it from an action that changes production state.

Required response:

- State the environment.
- State whether production state changed.
- Classify Friday staging preparation with no production-state change as staging preparation, not a production change.
- Classify an action that changes production state as a production change.

Scoring rule:

- Pass only when both classifications are correct and the responder cites the environment and whether production state changed as evidence.
- Friday staging preparation with no production-state change is not a production change.
- Any action that changes production state is a production change.
- Mark Partial when the label is correct but the environment/state evidence is missing or ambiguous.
- Mark Missed when staging preparation is treated as a production change or a production-state change is treated as staging preparation.

Facilitator record:

- Case A environment:
- Case A production state changed? Yes / No / Not recorded
- Case A classification:
- Case A evidence:
- Case B environment:
- Case B production state changed? Yes / No / Not recorded
- Case B classification:
- Case B evidence:
- Scenario 2 result: Pass / Partial / Missed

## Scenario 3 — Missing system control

Prompt to responder:
In the postmortem, identify the missing system control or guardrail that allowed the failure.

Required response:

- Name the absent control or guardrail.
- Describe the contributing system conditions.
- Identify the triggering operator action as the initiating action.
- Do not present the triggering operator action as the root cause.

Scoring rule:

- Pass when the responder identifies the missing control or guardrail and keeps the causal analysis focused on the absent control and contributing system conditions.
- Partial when a relevant system condition is identified but the control is incomplete or the causal boundary is unclear.
- Missed when the responder treats the triggering operator action as the root cause or fails to identify the missing control.
- Do not award credit for a blame statement that names only the operator action.

Facilitator record:

- Initiating operator action recorded:
- Missing control / guardrail identified:
- Contributing system conditions:
- Operator action kept distinct from root cause? Yes / No
- Nadia review notes:
- Scenario 3 result: Pass / Partial / Missed

## Session summary

- Participant / rotation:
- Exercise date and time:
- Facilitator:
- Wes responder-path notes:
- Nadia postmortem notes:
- Alex scenario/cross-service notes:
- Scenario 1 result: Pass / Partial / Missed
- Scenario 2 result: Pass / Partial / Missed
- Scenario 3 result: Pass / Partial / Missed
- Overall result: Pass / Follow-up / Rerun required
- Misses or unsupported assumptions:
- Relevant owner for follow-up:
- Follow-up due before next rotation exercise:
- Evidence links or timestamps:

## Closeout check

- Incident start time recorded.
- Secondary-engagement time recorded when isolation failed.
- Boundary result recorded; no inferred credit used.
- Environment and production-state evidence recorded for both classifications.
- Missing control identified without blaming the triggering operator action.
- Misses assigned to the relevant owner.
- Exercise remains training evidence only and does not authorize a production change.

I don't want it to read as if every high-cardinality label is automatically forbidden, and I want the rollup-service parity check plus the live-versus-validation alert boundary embedded directly in the checklist. Turn these notes into a practical PR/review checklist for the first Cardinality Guardrails control slice, with pass/fail language and explicit non-goals.

messages.content:
Cardinality Guardrails — First-pass PR/review checklist

Scope

Apply this checklist to any metrics-router or shard-keeper change that adds, removes, renames, or changes the meaning of a metric label.

This is a review control, not a universal ban on high-cardinality labels. A label may pass when its cardinality is intentionally justified, bounded or mitigated, and its operational impact is understood.

1. Change inventory and ownership

[ ] PASS — The PR lists every new or changed label key, the affected metric(s), the service being changed, and whether the change is an addition, rename, removal, or semantic change.

[ ] PASS — Each new or changed label has:
    - An explicit owner
    - A stated reason for existence
    - A description of what values it may contain
    - An indication of whether values are bounded, approximately bounded, or potentially unbounded

[ ] FAIL — Any label is introduced or materially changed without an owner, rationale, or value-domain description.

Reviewer evidence:
    - PR description or linked design note
    - Exact metric and label names
    - Owning team or service owner

2. Cardinality-risk review

[ ] PASS — The PR identifies whether each label is:
    - A bounded category
    - A moderately variable operational dimension
    - Raw or near-unique
    - Request-derived or otherwise potentially unbounded

[ ] PASS — The PR includes representative distinct-count samples for proposed labels such as route_pattern, when applicable. The sample includes its time window, traffic/sample basis, and limitations.

[ ] PASS — Sampled counts are used as risk evidence, not represented as exact production totals or a guarantee of future cardinality.

[ ] PASS — A label with elevated cardinality has an explicit disposition, such as:
    - Accepted because the value range is justified and operationally manageable
    - Bounded or normalized before emission
    - Aggregated or moved to a lower-cardinality representation
    - Deferred pending additional evidence
    - Rejected because the risk is unbounded or lacks mitigation

[ ] FAIL — The review rejects a label solely because it is “high cardinality,” without considering purpose, bounds, mitigation, and operational impact.

[ ] FAIL — The review accepts a raw identifier, near-unique value, or request-derived value without an explicit risk disposition and mitigation rationale.

[ ] FAIL — error_detail is added as a label.

Reviewer evidence:
    - Cardinality sample or query
    - Expected value-domain explanation
    - Mitigation or aggregation design, if needed
    - Cost/impact notes where relevant

3. Cross-service rollup-service parity

[ ] PASS — The PR explicitly states whether the label change crosses a boundary into rollup-service.

[ ] PASS — If it does cross that boundary, the PR includes a parity check covering the affected label names and meanings, including any relevant differences in:
    - Label presence or absence
    - Value shape or normalization
    - Aggregation behavior
    - Downstream query, alert, or dashboard assumptions

[ ] PASS — The parity check identifies the owner of the corresponding rollup-service behavior and records the result before merge.

[ ] FAIL — A label name or meaning is changed in metrics-router or shard-keeper and forwarded to rollup-service without confirming that the receiving service has compatible semantics.

[ ] FAIL — The PR relies on an unqualified “rollup” reference. The affected service must be named explicitly as rollup-service; do not substitute the deprecated metric-rollup service.

[ ] PASS — If the change does not cross into rollup-service, the PR says so explicitly rather than leaving parity status ambiguous.

Reviewer evidence:
    - Link to rollup-service metric or schema definition
    - Before/after label mapping
    - Parity owner and review result
    - Updated downstream query or alert references, where applicable

arguments.title: Staff IC evidence review — April 10
arguments.body:
Staff IC evidence review — April 10

1. Likely questions and concise answers

Q: What is the Staff-level evidence?
A: I define cross-service systems and ownership boundaries, then make the interfaces, failure modes, and escalation paths explicit so service owners can execute independently. The leverage is in the durable operating model, not in personally owning every implementation.

Q: How do you work with service owners?
A: I review cross-service invariants, failure modes, ownership seams, and escalation boundaries. Service owners retain implementation, telemetry, readiness, and release decisions.

Q: What is the concrete impact?
A: The work reduces ambiguity at service boundaries, makes failure handling and handoffs more predictable, and supports safer decisions across services. Examples include explicit admission/rejection behavior, rollback evidence, and clear ownership seams.

Q: Are you the go/no-go approver for these services?
A: No. I provide cross-service systems and boundary guidance; the service owner remains accountable for implementation, telemetry, readiness, and release decisions.

Q: What is the calibration result?
A: The Staff IC calibration is open and being evaluated for the next review cycle; I should describe the evidence and scope, not imply an outcome.

2. Evidence that demonstrates leverage through systems and boundaries

- Metrics-router: clarified admission semantics, retaining rejection at the 20,000-queue cap before admission rather than admitting and evicting; paired this with tests for retry signaling, FIFO/order, accepted/rejected/evicted/completed accounting, and recovery below cap.
- Metrics-router configuration: established explicit legacy/replacement-key behavior and safe reload semantics, including rejection without changing the active configuration or watcher.
- Wes preflight: defined pipeline-only checks around SHA/cohort, ±5% traffic, bounded resources and errors, and holds on rising memory or queue age.
- Ownership boundaries: distinguished deprecated/unowned metric-rollup from Cyrus-owned rollup-service; supported metrics-router canaries and ingest-edge staging rollbacks without taking ownership; required Alex/Cyrus-team pairing for shard-keeper.
- Review posture: focused on cross-service invariants, failure modes, ownership seams, and escalation boundaries while leaving implementation, telemetry, readiness, and release decisions with the responsible owners.

3. Phrases to avoid

- “I own all of the services involved.”
- “I delegated the implementation and remain accountable for their day-to-day operations.”
- “I approve every service’s readiness or production release.”
- “I am the go/no-go approver for the canary or rollback.”
- “The service owners execute my decisions.”
- “I have secured Staff calibration.”
- “I am being promoted to Staff.”
- “The Staff title is effective.”
- “The calibration outcome is already decided.”

Closing note: The calibration remains underway for the next review cycle, and no Staff title is effective.

messages.content:
Cardinality Guardrails — First-pass PR/review checklist

Scope

Apply this checklist to any metrics-router or shard-keeper change that adds, removes, renames, or changes the meaning of a metric label.

This is a review control, not a universal ban on high-cardinality labels. A label may pass when its cardinality is intentionally justified, bounded or mitigated, and its operational impact is understood.

1. Change inventory and ownership

[ ] PASS — The PR lists every new or changed label key, the affected metric(s), the service being changed, and whether the change is an addition, rename, removal, or semantic change.

[ ] PASS — Each new or changed label has:
    - An explicit owner
    - A stated reason for existence
    - A description of what values it may contain
    - An indication of whether values are bounded, approximately bounded, or potentially unbounded

[ ] FAIL — Any label is introduced or materially changed without an owner, rationale, or value-domain description.

Reviewer evidence:
    - PR description or linked design note
    - Exact metric and label names
    - Owning team or service owner

2. Cardinality-risk review

[ ] PASS — The PR identifies whether each label is:
    - A bounded category
    - A moderately variable operational dimension
    - Raw or near-unique
    - Request-derived or otherwise potentially unbounded

[ ] PASS — The PR includes representative distinct-count samples for proposed labels such as route_pattern, when applicable. The sample includes its time window, traffic/sample basis, and limitations.

[ ] PASS — Sampled counts are used as risk evidence, not represented as exact production totals or a guarantee of future cardinality.

[ ] PASS — A label with elevated cardinality has an explicit disposition, such as:
    - Accepted because the value range is justified and operationally manageable
    - Bounded or normalized before emission
    - Aggregated or moved to a lower-cardinality representation
    - Deferred pending additional evidence
    - Rejected because the risk is unbounded or lacks mitigation

[ ] FAIL — The review rejects a label solely because it is “high cardinality,” without considering purpose, bounds, mitigation, and operational impact.

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.
output.title: INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

# Cross-service gate exceptions — June 14 review

I define cross-service gates and escalation boundaries; I do not take over routine service operation or Iris's product interpretation.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.
- **Escalation condition:** A production rollback gate fires, including a permit leak, active-work limit violation, dropped accepted points, or the applicable sustained request-p99 threshold.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

- Product Engineering owns implementation.
- Alex owns the cross-system contract and failure-mode review.

- Bind tenant identity for every input, authority reference, cache object, trace, and rendered rehearsal result.

Product Engineering's combined-payload candidate copied the metrics-router operating limit and estimated cost into a Lantern-owned payload and attached an owner-map mutation endpoint. # Authority-record time semantics — March 18 brown-bag

## Authoritative source time
`source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

## Fail-closed behavior
If a required source timestamp is missing or malformed, downstream navigation fails closed to explicit unknown.

## Multiple authority references
When one card carries multiple authority references, each reference retains its own `source_timestamp`. An envelope time, render time, processing time, or newest retry time must not be substituted for any reference's authoritative source time.

## Unchanged boundaries
This discussion creates no ownership, implementation, release, approval, or customer-authorization change. The internal reference-only integration remains outside the Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.

Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

arguments.body:
# Cardinality Guardrails: label-change preflight first cut

This entry records the first acceptance-check pass for the Q4 Cardinality Guardrails work. It is not a mature program, a general telemetry rewrite, a customer-facing surface, or a legacy-aggregator retirement plan.

## Reviewer checklist

### 1. Scope the change
Pass if the PR says whether it touches metrics-router, shard-keeper, rollup-service, or a cross-service label boundary.
Fail if the PR changes label names or label value shapes without naming the affected service boundary.

### 2. New label keys or changed value shapes
Pass if every new label key or changed value shape names an owner, source, expected cardinality shape, and whether it is live-path or validation-only.
Fail if a new label can appear on live metrics-router or shard-keeper traffic without an owner and expected cardinality shape.

### 3. Risky label families
- `customer_id`: high-cardinality by nature, but expected and already budgeted when owner/source are clear. Do not fail solely because this label is high-cardinality.
- `experiment_id`: fail live router pushes unless new experiment labels are explicitly allowed and bounded.
- `route_pattern`: pass only when values are normalized route patterns; fail raw IDs or raw paths.
- `deployment_sha`: okay for canary visibility; fail noisy joins with per-request labels.
- `error_detail`: fail as a metrics label family. Raw error strings or payload fragments should not become metric labels.

### 4. Sample distinct counts before promotion
Pass if the reviewer can see sample distinct counts from realistic traffic for new or changed label value shapes.
Fail if the only evidence is a hand-wavy assertion that the canary is green.

### 5. Rollup-service parity before cross-service label-name changes
Pass if rollup-service expects the same label name and semantics before a label-name change crosses service boundaries.
Fail if metrics-router or shard-keeper ships a label-name change that downstream rollup-service consumers do not recognize.

### 6. Alert-source and rollback semantics
Pass if dashboards and alert text distinguish live metrics-router traffic from replay or mirror validation samples.
Live-path movement can start rollback discussion.
Replay or mirror validation movement is investigation evidence and Q4 controls input, not rollback criteria.
Fail if replay or mirror movement is described as a live rollback trigger.

## Ownership and non-goals
Service-level enforcement tradeoffs stay with Alex's side of the metrics pipeline. Cyrus and data platform can provide cost examples and validate cost intuition, but they do not own router or shard enforcement gates.

Non-goals: no customer-facing dashboard, no release-readiness score, no broad telemetry rewrite, no legacy-aggregator retirement claim, no default ownership change for enforcement, and no claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

## First-use review notes — Nov 8, 2023

These notes clarify how to apply the first-cut checklist. They do not make Cardinality Guardrails mature, complete, or a general telemetry rewrite.

- Local metrics-router visibility labels: require owner, source, expected cardinality shape, and evidence from live canary traffic or a representative live-path fixture when the value shape can change on the hot path. Rollup-service signoff is not required for labels that do not cross a service boundary.
- Cross-service label names or meaning changes: require rollup-service parity before promotion. A green metrics-router canary does not substitute for downstream consumers expecting the same label name and semantics.
- `route_pattern`: pass only for normalized route patterns. If a code path could emit raw account IDs, widget IDs, or raw paths on live traffic, reviewers need live-path evidence or a representative live-path fixture; replay validation alone is not enough.
- Replay or mirror validation panels: keep them visible as investigation evidence. Do not describe replay or mirror movement as live rollback criteria.
- Cost examples: keep them directional and advisory. Cyrus/data platform can validate cost intuition, but enforcement gates stay with the service owners.

input.body:
Request changes. The production behavior described is not safe/complete for deployment.environment:

1. Normalization: lowercasing alone is underspecified. Define and test the canonical normalization for mixed case and any surrounding whitespace (including empty/whitespace-only input), and ensure all three services use the same helper/path.
2. Missing input: emitting `unknown` is reasonable, but add explicit fixtures/tests for absent, null, empty, and whitespace-only values so they cannot diverge between services.
3. Invalid input: replacing the allowlist with “publish every supplied string” removes invalid-input handling. Arbitrary/unbounded strings should not be accepted as valid environment values; define the invalid-value behavior (normally map to `unknown` or reject) and test malformed, whitespace, and unexpected values.
4. Per-tenant cardinality: removing the three-value tenant limiter is a production cardinality regression. Keep a bounded per-tenant limit or provide an equivalent enforced bound with overflow behavior and metrics; add a high-cardinality test.
5. Three-service parity: add/point to parity tests covering valid values (including `qa`), normalization, missing, invalid, and limiter/overflow behavior for each of the three production services. The current summary does not demonstrate that all three services are changed consistently.

Please include the production configuration/rollout implications and verify the resulting emitted values and cardinality bounds before re-requesting review.

arguments.title: Mosaic capacity response — final closeout
arguments.body:
Mosaic capacity response — final closeout

Decision date

January 22, 2026

Reviewers

Hema, Wes, Cyrus, Roman, Nadia, and Alex

Final decision

The Mosaic Commerce scale-response cycle is closed. The qualifying staged evidence and the January 20 production observation were reviewed together. No additional queue design, configuration change, or production push was made, and no capacity-related production window remains open.

Evidence reviewed

- Qualifying 90-minute staged replay at 19.78 million data points per minute.
- January 20 production observation at 17.2 million data points per minute.
- In production, every accepted batch reached exactly one terminal result and none was lost.
- Queue-wait p99 reached 302 milliseconds.
- Retryable queue-full responses reached 0.14%.
- The highest tenant reached 60 pending batches.
- Consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper lease, rollup-service, and full-health checks remained at baseline.

Production control

The production control is unchanged:

- Global queue: 2,048 batches.
- Per-tenant pending-batch limit: 64 batches.
- Excess work: retryable pre-acceptance backpressure.

Ownership and boundaries

- Wes remains the routine metrics-router decision-maker.
- Alex remains backup and reviews triggered cross-service invariant or failure-mode exceptions.
- The closeout does not transfer mapped service ownership or create a centralized approval requirement.

Forward qualification rule

For any later forecast above 17.2 million data points per minute, the mapped owners must first complete a fresh 90-minute replay at 15% above that forecast using the forecast's tenant distribution, batch-size distribution, and burst pattern.

The replay qualifies only if all of the following hold throughout the required evidence window:

- Queue-wait p99 does not exceed 400 milliseconds for five consecutive minutes.
- Retryable queue-full responses do not exceed 0.5% for five consecutive minutes.
- No tenant exceeds 64 pending batches.
- No accepted batch is lost.
- Consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper lease, rollup-service, and full-health checks remain at baseline.

This closeout records the final disposition of the current 17.2 million data points per minute forecast. Any later forecast above that level requires the fresh replay and all stated checks before any further capacity decision.

Mosaic capacity note

The first Mosaic-shaped replay, run at 18.4 million data points per minute against the original 16.0-million forecast peak, recorded queue-wait p99 of 230 ms and retryable queue-full responses of 0.07%. The later 90-minute staged replay, run at 19.78 million data points per minute against the revised 17.2-million forecast, recorded queue-wait p99 of 319 ms and retryable queue-full responses of 0.17%; the highest tenant reached 62 pending batches. Consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper lease, rollup-service, and full-health checks remained at baseline; cross-service review found no invariant or failure-mode exception.

Capacity conclusion: the first replay showed margin above the 16.0-million forecast; the later replay extended that staged evidence to the revised 17.2-million forecast with all acceptance and cross-service checks passing. The later replay did not authorize production. Direct production evidence and a subsequent closeout decision were still required.
