arguments.body:
Lantern platform boundary decision record — March 26 strategy review

Decision date: March 26, 2026
Decision effective date: April 1, 2026
Decision-makers: Hema and Theo

Decision

After reviewing the frozen operating evidence and the divergent Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce requests, Lantern will become a Sphere product-platform line effective April 1, 2026, rather than remain only a narrow add-on.

The existing authorization and operating terms remain unchanged through March 31, 2026. The new direction, role split, and access terms below apply on and after April 1, 2026.

Frozen operating evidence reviewed

The review included the frozen Lantern continuation-monitoring exports for November 2025, December 2025, and January 2026:

- November 2025: 805 sessions, 156 logical requests, 104 eligible combined requests, 34 separate requests with a source-timestamp gap greater than 24 hours, 18 explicit-unknown results, and 0 renderer failures.
- December 2025: 708 sessions, 137 logical requests, 91 eligible combined requests, 29 separate requests with a source-timestamp gap greater than 24 hours, 17 explicit-unknown results, and 0 renderer failures.
- January 2026: 732 sessions, 141 logical requests, 94 eligible combined requests, 31 separate requests with a source-timestamp gap greater than 24 hours, 16 explicit-unknown results, and 0 renderer failures.

Across all three frozen exports, the evidence showed no authorization-wrapper bypass, adapter call after denial, cross-tenant or excluded-field exposure, missing provenance or source timestamp, unpublished ownership render, read-only enforcement loss, or other automatic-stop condition.

Operating boundary and role split effective April 1

- Iris owns the customer promise, adoption criteria, and UI interpretation.
- Alex retains freshness, tenant-isolation, authorization-denial, latency, and error monitoring, plus the shared data contract, source-registration safety gates, and failure-mode review.
- Product Engineering owns implementation.
- Lantern explains provenance-backed service and system state.
- Cardinality Guardrails owns pipeline limits and cost signals.
- The owner map remains the source of published responsibility.

Lantern will not produce release-readiness judgments or employee-performance interpretations.

Source-registration safety requirements

Any new source type must enter through shared registration with all of the following before customer use:

- tenant-scoped authorization before source access;
- required provenance and source timestamps;
- explicit unknown when input is stale or missing;
- excluded-field checks; and
- a successful safety rerun.

Authorized access: April 1 through September 30, 2026

Only Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce are authorized for continued read-only access through the shared authorization wrapper. No other account is authorized. Access is limited to:

- provenance-backed deploy movement;
- published service ownership;
- timestamped incident-load summaries; and
- explicit unknown states.

The following remain unauthorized: additional accounts, cost data, CSV export, raw incident text, internal room metadata, employee identifiers or comparisons, inferred or unpublished ownership, internal-only fallback data, and any write capability.

Automatic suspension conditions

An authorization-wrapper bypass, adapter call after denial, cross-tenant material, stale or missing source rendered as anything other than explicit unknown, a deploy event without required provenance, unpublished ownership, an incident-load summary without its source timestamp, exposure of any excluded field, or loss of read-only enforcement immediately suspends both authorized accounts pending correction and a successful rerun of the affected safety check.

Latency and other errors do not independently suspend access unless they cause one of the violations above.

Ownership and review boundary

This record establishes the April 1 product-platform transition while preserving the current operating terms through March 31. The owner map is authoritative for published responsibility, and the stated authorization, provenance, isolation, freshness, denial, read-only, and failure-mode boundaries remain the controlling safeguards.

Scope and status

arguments.query: "Q1 2027 platform workstreams"

arguments.body:
Q1 2027 working brief

Purpose
Carry the approved Q1 structure into planning as three linked workstreams—not a single Lantern backlog. Each workstream has a distinct purpose, mapped owner, and handoff boundary.

Linked workstreams and mapped owners

1. Lantern — explanation and navigation
Purpose: Help cards explain and navigate to authoritative ownership and Cardinality Guardrails records without becoming a second source of truth.
Mapped owner: Product Engineering owns Lantern implementation, release, and operations.

2. Cardinality Guardrails — pipeline limits and cost semantics
Purpose: Define and maintain the authoritative pipeline limits and cost semantics that Lantern can reference.
Mapped owner: Infra owns the Guardrails implementation, release, rollback, and operations.

3. Owner map — published responsibility
Purpose: Publish and maintain the authoritative responsibility records that identify the service/team ownership Lantern navigates to.
Mapped owner: The owner-map team owns publication, updates, and operations for those responsibility records.

Shared reference contract and handoff points
Lantern cards may reference authoritative records using only these five fields:
- tenant_id
- canonical_service_id
- authority_type
- authority_record_id
- source_timestamp

The contract is reference-only: Lantern may navigate to the authoritative Owner Map or Cardinality Guardrails record, but must not copy or mutate its payload. The source system remains responsible for the meaning, freshness, and lifecycle of its record.

Handoffs:
- Owner Map and Guardrails publish the authoritative record and its source_timestamp.
- Lantern consumes the five-field reference to explain or navigate; it does not recreate the record.
- Any contract, freshness, identity, or cross-system failure is surfaced at the shared boundary and routed to the owning system.
- Harbor Health and Mosaic remain excluded unless separately authorized.

Planning and review boundaries
Product Engineering remains responsible for Lantern implementation; this structure does not transfer that responsibility into a shared Lantern backlog or make Alex the implementation gate.

Alex reviews the shared contract and cross-system failure boundaries: field meaning, authority, identity, freshness, and handoff behavior across Lantern, Guardrails, and the owner map. Alex does not review or approve every implementation decision. The mapped teams own implementation, release, rollback, and operations for their workstreams.

Kickoff preparation — January 7, 2027 decision session

Purpose

Treat the kickoff as a decision session, not a broad status review. The approved split remains unchanged:
- Lantern owns explanation and navigation.
- Cardinality Guardrails owns pipeline limits and cost semantics.
- The owner map owns published responsibility.

Interfaces requiring agreement

- Boundary between Lantern explanation/navigation and Cardinality Guardrails pipeline-limit and cost-semantics behavior: what each workstream exposes, what it does not, and how a user follows an explanation to the authoritative source.
- Boundary between each workstream and the owner map: which responsibility records are authoritative, how ownership is identified, and how changes are handed off for publication.
- Cross-workstream identifiers and references: the minimum stable fields needed to navigate between authoritative records without copying or mutating their payloads.
- Failure and ambiguity handling: what happens when an owner, authority record, source timestamp, limit, or cost value is missing, stale, malformed, or disputed; which team records the exception and which owner resolves it.
- Evidence and change handoff: acceptance criteria, source timestamps, rollback or correction path, and the point at which an implementation is ready for owner-map publication.

Handoff evidence for each mapped owner

Each mapped owner should bring:
- the authoritative record or source reference and its source timestamp;
- the named service/workstream responsibility and explicit boundary with adjacent owners;
- the interface fields and invariants the receiving workstream may rely on;
- representative success, missing, stale, malformed, and disputed cases;
- acceptance evidence (tests, sample traces, or replay results as applicable);
- operational ownership for release, rollback, correction, and escalation; and
- the proposed publication/update path for the owner map.

First-deliverable decisions for January 7

Decide, not merely review:
- the first deliverable for Lantern: [OPEN — participant proposal pending];
- the first deliverable for Cardinality Guardrails: [OPEN — participant proposal pending];
- the first deliverable for the owner map: [OPEN — participant proposal pending];
- the minimum acceptance evidence and owner handoff required for each first deliverable;
- the sequence and dependencies among the three deliverables; and
- the decision owners, target dates, and escalation path for unresolved interface questions.

Kickoff proposals — pending January 7 decisions

The following proposals are recorded for the January 7 decision session. They are proposals only, pending the decisions; they are not approved deliverables, commitments, or ownership changes:

- Iris proposes an internal interpretation and wording check for Lantern’s reference navigation.
- Cyrus proposes a versioned Cardinality Guardrails authority-record interface that keeps pipeline limits and cost semantics authoritative in Guardrails.
- Wes proposes an inventory mapping metrics-router operating controls to their authoritative records and current operating evidence.
- Product Engineering proposes the first Lantern implementation slice consuming those references without copying authority values or adding mutation.

Alex’s bounded review role

Alex’s contribution remains limited to review of the five-field shared contract and cross-system failure boundaries. This bounded review role is not an implementation, release, rollback, operations, or centralized approval responsibility, and does not change mapped ownership. It is recorded alongside the proposals for January 7 discussion, not as an approved deliverable or ownership change.

Status: all four items above remain proposals pending the January 7 decisions. No proposal above changes the approved workstream split, mapped ownership, or routine implementation responsibility.

Scope boundary

Customer authorization is out of scope for this kickoff and these workstreams; no customer authorization is implied by the interfaces or navigation described here. Routine implementation ownership is also out of scope: mapped teams retain implementation, release, rollback, and operational ownership, while this session agrees shared interfaces, evidence, and published responsibility boundaries. The kickoff does not create a centralized approval gate unless separately assigned.

bookend_start.content: [2024-12-24T17:20:00-05:00] Cyrus asked for a second look at a rollup-service queue alert during a holiday traffic burst. Queue age rose from 45 seconds to 6 minutes while incoming accepted points increased 31%, but consumer throughput stayed flat rather than falling. Rollup errors are zero, metrics-router and ingest-edge health remain at baseline, and queue age started declining once input returned to normal. Help me classify this evidence, identify the checks needed before closing the alert as bounded consumer-capacity backlog, and separate Data Platform follow-up from any Infra concern without shifting rollup ownership to Infra.

arguments.query: rollup queue backlog consumer throughput queue age alert close checks

messages.content:
Classification

This is best classified as a valid rollup-service queue-age alert caused by a bounded consumer-capacity backlog during a traffic burst—not as a rollup failure and not as an Infra incident.

Evidence supporting that classification:

- Queue age crossed the five-minute alert threshold, rising from 45 seconds to six minutes.
- Accepted input increased by 31%.
- Consumer throughput stayed flat, indicating a consumer-capacity ceiling or saturation point rather than a sudden consumer failure.
- Rollup errors remained at zero.
- metrics-router and ingest-edge stayed at baseline, so there is no evidence of upstream degradation.
- Queue age began declining when input returned to normal, which argues against an uncontrolled backlog, stuck consumer, or continuing resource leak.

The alert was therefore real and actionable, but the observed condition appears bounded and self-recovering.

Checks before closing

Close only after confirming all of the following:

1. Backlog recovery
   - Queue age is below the alert threshold and continues to decline.
   - Backlog depth and oldest-item age are draining, not merely oscillating.
   - The backlog reaches the normal operating range and remains there for a sustained observation period after input normalization.

2. Consumer health
   - Consumers are processing normally with no crash loop, restart increase, stuck partition/shard, or loss of assignment.
   - Throughput is consistent with the configured consumer/concurrency limit.
   - There is no growing retry, dead-letter, rebalance, or poison-item signal.
   - CPU, memory, I/O, broker, and connection metrics show capacity pressure if expected, but no fault condition or continuing resource slope.

3. Data integrity
   - Accepted points, processed points, and rollup outputs reconcile within the expected accounting window.
   - Dropped, rejected, duplicated, or permanently failed points remain at their normal values.
   - There is no delayed or missing output after the queue drains.

4. Dependency confirmation
   - metrics-router and ingest-edge remain at baseline for accepted throughput, latency, errors, drops, and backpressure.
   - Their health is corroborating evidence only; it should not suppress or redefine the rollup queue-age alert.

5. Alert behavior
   - The alert clears naturally after queue age remains below threshold.
   - No second queue-age rise occurs after traffic returns to its normal level.
   - Record the burst magnitude, maximum queue age, flat consumer throughput, zero-error result, recovery point, and confirmation that integrity checks passed.

If queue age stops declining, rises again at normal input, consumer throughput falls below its normal cap, or integrity/retry/restart signals worsen, do not close it as bounded backlog. Continue investigating rollup-service.

Ownership split

Data Platform / Cyrus team follow-up:

- Own the alert closure and incident record for rollup-service; the runbook identifies Cyrus’s team as the owner.
- Confirm whether the flat throughput reflects an intentional configured consumer limit.
- Review holiday-burst capacity headroom, consumer concurrency, partition/shard parallelism, and scaling behavior.

arguments.title: Lantern pilot-preparation agreement
arguments.body:
Lantern pilot-preparation agreement

Date: 2024-12-11
Status: Preparation only; no pilot customer selected and customer access remains closed.

Purpose

This agreement records the decision to move Lantern out of blocker-remediation mode and into pilot preparation. It does not authorize customer access, select a customer, or constitute a production rollout approval.

Evidence basis

- The authorized 30-day internal shadow was completed.
- The shadow covered 18,400 customer-shaped lookups across two synthetic tenants and selected Infra/Product Engineering release-review traffic.
- The evidence was technical only; customer access remains closed.
- The shadow met all four agreed conditions:
  1. No cross-tenant material was observed.
  2. Eleven stale permitted-source cases rendered explicit unknown rather than returning stale ownership.
  3. Denied requests made no adapter calls.
  4. No external field used internal room metadata.
- Iris found the resulting cards understandable without exposing omitted internal sources.
- Based on this completed evidence, Theo asked Lantern to move out of blocker-remediation mode, and Hema agreed that it is technically qualified for pilot preparation.

Role split

Iris — customer interpretation and selection criteria

- Own the customer-facing interpretation of the evidence and any pilot-readiness language intended for customer review.
- Define and document customer selection criteria.
- Confirm that any proposed customer and use case fit the approved criteria before any access decision is considered.
- Keep customer selection separate from the technical qualification recorded here.

Alex — monitoring, provenance failure behavior, and operational handoff

- Own monitoring requirements, dashboards/alerts, and review thresholds for preparation and any later pilot gate.
- Own provenance failure behavior, including explicit unknown/unavailable handling when permitted ownership data is stale or unavailable, and fail-closed behavior for denied or expired authorization.
- Confirm that source and observation timestamps, source_system, and source_ref remain available where required by the contract.
- Prepare the operational handoff: runbook, escalation path, incident ownership, rollback/stop conditions, and evidence needed for a later go/no-go decision.

Shared boundary

- Neither role assignment authorizes customer access or selects a customer.
- Technical qualification is not customer approval, launch approval, or a broad-rollout decision.
- Any disagreement about interpretation, criteria, monitoring, provenance behavior, or handoff readiness is a gate to resolve before advancing.

Pilot-preparation checklist

Customer interpretation and selection — Iris

[ ] Write the customer-facing interpretation of the shadow evidence without overstating it as customer validation.
[ ] Define inclusion and exclusion criteria for a potential pilot customer and use case.
[ ] Define the evidence and approvals required before naming any customer.
[ ] Confirm that proposed scenarios do not require exposing omitted internal sources or internal room metadata.
[ ] Record that no customer is selected at this stage.

Monitoring and operational readiness — Alex

[ ] Specify pilot-preparation monitoring signals, dashboards, alert thresholds, and review cadence.
[ ] Specify how stale, missing, denied, or expired provenance/authorization is rendered and logged.
[ ] Verify fail-closed behavior for denied or expired authorization and no adapter calls on denied requests.
[ ] Verify explicit unknown/unavailable ownership when the owner map is beyond the 24-hour freshness limit; do not infer ownership from stale data.
[ ] Verify tenant isolation and authorized-only data handling.
[ ] Confirm required provenance fields and timestamps remain present in outputs and operational records.
[ ] Draft or update the runbook, escalation path, incident contacts, and operational handoff checklist.
[ ] Define stop/rollback conditions and the evidence required to pass each later gate.

Joint gates before any customer-access decision

[ ] Iris has approved the customer interpretation and selection criteria.
[ ] Alex has approved monitoring, provenance failure behavior, and the operational handoff.
[ ] Technical and customer-readiness evidence are recorded separately.
[ ] A named customer has not been treated as selected until a separate explicit decision is made.
[ ] Customer access remains closed until the required approvals and access decision are completed.

Closed-access boundary

- No customer is selected.
- No customer access is open or implied by this agreement.
- No customer data, customer credentials, or customer-connected adapter calls are authorized by this agreement.
- The completed shadow is technical evidence only and does not substitute for customer approval, customer-specific authorization, privacy/security review, or a separate pilot go/no-go decision.
- Internal synthetic-tenant and authorized internal release-review evidence must not be represented as customer usage or customer validation.
- Lantern remains in preparation: the next work is to complete the checklist and record the separate decisions required before any pilot-access change.

messages.content:
Three narrow success signals Theo can use:

1. Provenance is understood
   - In a short scenario, users can correctly identify what a Lantern signal came from—its source, timestamp, event type, or backend state—and distinguish live-path evidence from replay/mirror validation.
   - Success looks like: users explain “where this came from” without asking Lantern to ingest raw incident notes or treating validation evidence as a rollback trigger.

2. Permission wording sets the right boundary
   - Users can accurately answer what Lantern is permitted to show and what it deliberately does not show.
   - Success looks like: they understand that bounded, permission-scoped signals are the product—not a missing feature to work around—and do not request broader access or manual owner-card overrides.

3. Empty states are interpreted as intentional
   - When a signal is unavailable, users recognize the empty state as “not shown from permitted or verified sources,” rather than as a failure, an implied problem, or an invitation to fill in the gap themselves.
   - Success looks like: users choose the appropriate next step—leave it unresolved or consult an authorized source—without inferring release readiness, adding incident notes, or overriding ownership manually.

A simple feedback format would be one comprehension question per signal, using fixed scenarios and multiple-choice answers plus an optional explanation. That measures whether the boundaries are understood without rewarding broader Lantern usage.

It should begin after an action has already been accepted, require responders to preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication, identify Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner, and confine a triggered failure-mode reviewer to that boundary. arguments.body:
Purpose
Run the timed incident handoff and response scenarios as Hema's quarterly infra-rotation onboarding module. Keep this entry separate from the existing "Rotation handoff" entry.

Scenario checks
1. Incident clock and secondary engagement
   - Start and record the incident clock.
   - When isolation fails, verify that the secondary is engaged before the 45-minute boundary.
   - Record the engagement time and whether the boundary was met; do not award credit from an unrecorded or inferred handoff.

2. Change classification
   - Classify Friday staging preparation with no production-state change as staging preparation, not a production change.
   - Distinguish it from an action that changes production state, which must be classified as a production change.
   - State the environment and whether production state changed as evidence for the classification.

3. Missing system control
   - In the postmortem, identify the missing system control or guardrail that allowed the failure.
   - Do not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause; describe it as the initiating action and keep the analysis focused on the absent control and contributing system conditions.

4. Cross-service failure case: production-ramp evidence boundary
   Scenario prompt:
   - During a scheduled production ramp, metrics-router queue-wait p99 and retryable queue-full responses remain below their numeric stop thresholds, tenant pending batches remain within the configured limit, and route consistency, dropped-series, shard-keeper lease health, rollup-service parity, and the full health set remain at baseline.
   - The observation shows no accepted points lost.
   - The instrumentation preserves insufficient batch identity to determine whether any accepted batch was lost.
   - No production change or rollback is made during the observation.
   - Ask the responder to state the evidence boundary, classify the environment/state, name the missing control, and decide whether the broader scale-response cycle can close or another production window can be opened.

   Facilitator key — bounded answer:
   - Point-level evidence supports only the bounded statement that no accepted points were observed lost. It cannot establish that no accepted batch was lost, so the accepted-batch-loss stop condition is not clean and must not be marked passed.
   - Name the instrumentation gap precisely: accepted-batch identity is not preserved end-to-end, preventing reconciliation of accepted batches across the cross-service path. Do not infer a batch-loss result, fill in missing identifiers, or claim that the batch-level condition passed.
   - Record the observation as production traffic/production observation with no production state change made by the responders; do not relabel it as staging preparation or claim a deploy, rollback, or traffic shift occurred.
   - Keep the broader scale-response cycle open. Do not authorize another production window. The next decision requires the missing batch-identity evidence/control and the existing bounded acceptance and baseline checks; it is not authorized by the point-level result alone.
   - Preserve the existing queue, tenant, backpressure, stop-condition, and owner boundaries. This case tests evidence sufficiency and cross-service control coverage, not a new queue design or a transfer of operational ownership.

5. Q3 incident-practice scenario: bounded tenant label correction
   Scenario prompt:
   - In staging, the completed bounded-label correction emits: tenant_size_class="17342".
   - Responders must identify the allowed invariant for tenant_size_class as exactly one of: small, medium, large, or unknown. The numeric value "17342" is not an allowed published label value; treat it as an invariant-boundary trigger requiring the bounded correction path, not as a recurring rollup-service gate.
   - Keep the raw tenant hash only in debug logs. Do not publish, retain in normal operational output, or use the raw tenant hash as a responder-facing label.
   - Route implementation, release, and rollback to Roman. Do not assign those actions to Alex or turn this completed correction into a standing recurring rollup-service review or gate.
   - Engage Alex only when the allowed-label invariant boundary is triggered. Ordinary handling of the completed correction does not require Alex engagement.

   Staging output:
   - tenant_size_class="17342"

   Facilitator key — bounded answer:
   - The allowed invariant is the bounded label set {small, medium, large, unknown}; "17342" violates that published invariant and is the explicit trigger for the boundary path.
   - Preserve the raw tenant hash only in debug logs and keep it out of normal responder-facing or published output.
   - Roman owns implementation, release, and rollback. Alex is engaged only for the triggered invariant boundary, not for a recurring rollup-service gate or routine rollup-service review.
   - Preserve this as one Q3 incident-practice scenario documenting the completed correction; do not convert it into a recurring rollup-service control.

6. November 18, 2027 incident-practice scenario: cancellation or caller disconnect after acceptance
   Scenario type: executable tabletop/drill only. This is not a production procedure, production window, deploy, release, rollback, or ownership change.

   Setup and start condition:
   - Schedule and run the exercise on November 18, 2027.
   - Begin only after a metrics-router action has already been accepted by the service. The responder must record the acceptance event and create or retrieve one durable attempt identity before injecting any fault.
   - Use a non-production fixture or harness. Do not send production traffic, alter production state, open a production window, deploy, release, or roll back.

   Responder procedure:
   1. At acceptance, persist exactly one attempt record keyed by the durable attempt identity. The identity must survive cancellation, caller disconnect, process restart/recovery, retries, and publication. Do not create a second attempt identity during recovery.
   2. Inject cancellation after acceptance, then exercise caller disconnect while the accepted action is still unresolved. The responder path must treat cancellation and disconnect as delivery/lifecycle events, not as permission to discard accepted work or start a replacement attempt.
   3. Force process loss and recover the worker from durable state. On recovery, look up the existing attempt identity, resume or finalize that attempt, and reject any duplicate recovery-created attempt.
   4. Drive the attempt to one terminal result. Record the terminal result durably before publication, and make finalization idempotent: repeated cancellation, disconnect, recovery, or retry signals must not create another terminal result.
   5. Publish the caller-visible result, including after the original caller has disconnected, from the same durable attempt record. Publication retries may repeat delivery of that result but may not create a new terminal outcome.

   Required assertions and evidence:
   - One durable attempt identity is present from acceptance through cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication; show the identity at each boundary.
   - Exactly one terminal result exists for the accepted action. Reconcile accepted work to that result and show no duplicate, missing, or conflicting terminal result.
   - A disconnected caller does not cause accepted work to be lost, duplicated, or re-accepted. A cancellation request does not erase the accepted attempt.
   - Recovery reuses the durable identity and does not publish a second outcome. Publication is at-least-retry-safe for delivery while remaining exactly one terminal result for the attempt.
   - Capture the acceptance, cancellation, disconnect, process-loss, recovery, finalization, and publication evidence, plus the final durable record and reconciliation result. A missing boundary event or ambiguous identity is a failed exercise, not a pass by inference.

   Ownership and review boundaries:
   - Wes is the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner. Wes teaches the responder path for this exercise; those ownership mappings remain unchanged.
   - A failure-mode reviewer is triggered only if the exercise exposes a cross-service invariant, provenance, or failure-mode exception at the metrics-router boundary. Confine that reviewer to reviewing the triggered boundary; do not turn the exercise into a standing approval gate or routine reviewer role.
   - Nadia reviews the postmortem section, including the missing-control analysis and the evidence for exactly one terminal result.
   - Alex maintains the bounded cross-service failure case and may review only the triggered failure-mode boundary described above. Alex does not become the implementation, release, or rollback owner.

   Facilitator key — bounded answer:
   - The exercise starts after acceptance, so the accepted action must retain one durable attempt identity even when cancellation and caller disconnect occur.
   - Process recovery and publication must converge on that same identity and exactly one terminal result. Repeated signals or publication retries are not additional attempts or terminal outcomes.
   - Mark the exercise failed if accepted work is dropped, duplicated, re-accepted under a new identity, or left without exactly one terminal result; also fail it if the result is published without durable finalization or if recovery cannot prove identity continuity.
   - Treat this as a non-production practice scenario only. It creates no production procedure or window, makes no deploy/release/rollback decision, and changes no ownership.

Roles
- Wes teaches the responder path and the incident-clock/secondary-engagement portion.
- Nadia reviews the postmortem section, including the missing-control analysis and the November 18 exactly-one-terminal-result evidence.
- Alex maintains the bounded cross-service failure cases and updates scenarios when dependencies or failure modes change; Alex is engaged only at a triggered failure-mode boundary.
- Roman owns implementation, release, and rollback for the completed Q3 bounded-label correction; Alex's role is limited to the triggered invariant boundary described in that scenario.

Cadence and evidence
Run this module quarterly for each infra rotation. Capture the incident start time, secondary-engagement time, isolation outcome, change classification with environment/state evidence, and the identified missing control. For the production-ramp case, also capture the exact evidence boundary, whether accepted-batch identity was preserved, whether the accepted-batch stop condition can be marked clean, and whether the broader scale-response cycle remains open. For the Q3 bounded-label scenario, capture the exact staging output tenant_size_class="17342", the identified allowed invariant set, confirmation that the raw tenant hash remained debug-only, the Roman implementation/release/rollback routing, and whether Alex was engaged only because the invariant boundary triggered. For the November 18 scenario, capture the acceptance, cancellation, disconnect, process-loss, recovery, finalization, and publication events; the single durable attempt identity at every boundary; the single terminal result; the reconciliation showing no duplicate or missing accepted work; and any triggered failure-mode review. Review misses with the relevant owner before the next rotation exercise.

August 5 executed outcome
- The Q3 tabletop executed the bounded tenant-label correction scenario. The staging output tenant_size_class="17342" violated the bounded invariant requiring exactly one of small, medium, large, or unknown.
- The raw value remained out of metric labels and normal responder-facing output.
- Wes taught the responder path. Nadia focused the postmortem discussion on the missing guardrail rather than blame.
- Alex reviewed only the triggered invariant boundary. Roman retained implementation, release, and rollback decisions.
- No production, release, or ownership decision was made by this exercise.

September 8, 2027 explicit-unknown ownership practice case
- Scenario prompt: the authoritative owner map returns explicit unknown for the affected ownership lookup, while an automation proposes assigning Alex as the fallback operational owner.
- Responder requirement: keep ownership explicitly unknown and the work unassigned. Do not accept the automation's fallback proposal as an ownership determination.

- Annual premium: $104 × 26 paychecks = $2,704
- Premium plus out-of-pocket maximum: $2,704 + $4,800 = $7,504
- Net of Sphere’s $900 HSA funding: $7,504 − $900 = $6,604

arguments.body:
ingest-edge cutover playbook

Scope
- This runbook covers the current ingest-edge deployment and production cutover flow.
- legacy-aggregator is not part of the ingest-edge path. Do not use its routing, validation, or incident-response steps here.

1. Prepare
- Confirm the ingest-edge version and deployment configuration are ready for release.
- Review dashboards and alert coverage for ingest-edge before the cutover.
- Schedule staging cutovers for Monday morning; reserve Friday afternoons for review and preparation rather than deployment.

2. Validate in staging
- Deploy the candidate ingest-edge version to staging.
- Exercise the ingest-edge flow and confirm events are processed successfully.
- Check ingest-edge latency, error rate, throughput, and dropped-event signals before proceeding.

3. Cut over production
- Deploy the validated version to production during the approved window.
- Monitor ingest-edge dashboards and alerts continuously for the first 90 minutes.
- Confirm there are no event drops and that latency and error rates remain at their expected baseline.

4. Complete the observation check
- For the v2.19.4 cutover, continue monitoring through the formal 48-hour production check, due April 4, 2024.
- Confirm there are no dropped events, latency or error-rate regressions, or Prometheus anomalies.
- If the checks are clean, mark the cutover complete and file the close-out note.

5. Incident handling
- For an ingest-edge issue, use the ingest-edge dashboards, alerts, logs, and escalation path. Do not fall back to legacy-aggregator procedures.
- Record the observed impact, affected version, timeline, and mitigation in the cutover close-out or incident record.

Service note — OTel collector 0.91 rollout (2023-07-27)
- Production-clean after the heightened watch: error rate and CPU stayed flat.
- p95 memory settled about 5% above the pre-bump collector baseline, still within normal headroom.
- Future collector bumps still require staging replay plus an explicit memory watch.

Service note — OTel exporter retry-only change (sha:0a91b7c)
- This note covers the exporter retry change only; it is not a collector-wide tuning guide.
- Exporter retry max_interval is 15 seconds.
- Exporter retry max_elapsed_time is 5 minutes.
- Memory-limiter settings were deliberately not part of this patch.
- After deployment, check dropped writes, backpressure counters, and retry log volume.

## OTel exporter retry-only change — Oct 2023 note

For the retry-only OTel collector change deployed as `sha:0a91b7c`, the operational intent was to reduce staging/prod exporter retry noise without hiding real pressure signals.

Settings in scope:
- `max_interval`: 15 seconds
- `max_elapsed_time`: 5 minutes

Settings explicitly out of scope:
- Memory-limiter settings were not changed in this patch.

Post-deploy checks:
- Dropped writes should stay at zero.
- Backpressure counters should remain visible.
- Exporter retry log volume should decrease, but not by suppressing real backpressure evidence.

If dropped writes appear or backpressure counters disappear, treat that as a signal problem rather than a successful noise reduction.

## Staging-drill hygiene — 2024-01-03 after-action

Before opening the deploy-pipeline staging lane for an ingest-edge rollback drill:
- Verify the load-test tag TTL.
- Confirm the cleanup owner for the load-test tag and related staging artifacts.
- Do not open the staging lane until both the TTL and cleanup owner are explicitly verified.

Dec 22 boundaries:
- This guidance applies to the deploy-pipeline path only.
- Wes can perform the daylight first pass for this staging-drill class.
- Escalate unsafe or ambiguous signals rather than proceeding on assumption.
- This does not change production ownership or the owner map.

## Production behavior and v2.19.4 cutover record — 2024-04-02

- ingest-edge v2.19.4 is at 100% production after the full-production observation completed cleanly.
- Randomized one-to-three-second `Retry-After` behavior is now the production behavior for 429 responses; do not describe it as canary-only or restore the baseline behavior solely because the observation completed.
- The formal 48-hour production check remains due April 4, 2024.
- Synchronized retry bursts did not reform after 429 responses during the 50% gate.

Explicit stop boundaries for this cutover
Immediately stop the rollout, hold further promotion, and prepare rollback if any one of the following occurs:
- Any increase in 5xx responses.
- p99 latency at or above 190 ms.
- Queue depth at or above 76%.
- Accepted-throughput loss at or above 3% versus baseline.
- Retry volume at or above 130,000 attempts per second.

Observed gate maxima
- 10% gate: peak retries 123,000 attempts per second; p99 172 ms; queue depth 74%; accepted throughput 2.4% below baseline; no 5xx increase.
- 50% gate: peak retries 128,000 attempts per second; p99 186 ms; queue depth 75%; accepted throughput 2.8% below baseline; no 5xx increase.
- 100% gate/full-production observation: peak retries 129,000 attempts per second; p99 188 ms; queue depth 75%; accepted throughput 2.9% below baseline; no 5xx increase.

All production gates passed. Keep v2.19.4 at 100% and retain the randomized one-to-three-second `Retry-After` behavior as production behavior. The explicit stop boundaries remain in force through the formal 48-hour check.

## Production tenant-fair queue behavior — 2024-07-05

The mapped owner completed the remaining ingest-edge rollout. At both the 50% gate and full production:
- Repeated noisy-tenant tests preserved the eight-waiting cap per tenant.
- Newly queued low-volume tenants entered the ring immediately.
- Work-conserving dispatch used each eligible slot.
- Empty tenants were removed from the ring after cancellation.
- Every queue-cap response retained `Retry-After`.
- Existing active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, and restart checks remained clean.

Preserve these existing ingest-edge requirements during cutover, operation, and rollback:
- No more than four active work items per pod.
- No more than two active work items per tenant.
- Bounded decompression must remain enforced.
- Retry behavior and its existing requirements must remain enforced, including retaining `Retry-After` on queue-cap responses.

Treat any loss of the eight-waiting cap, delayed ring admission for newly queued low-volume tenants, unused eligible dispatch capacity, failure to remove empty tenants after cancellation, missing `Retry-After`, or regression in active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, or restart checks as a rollout/operational signal requiring investigation before further promotion.

## Bounded service-discovery membership check — May 24 zone imbalance

Use this bounded check when a zone imbalance or similar service-discovery membership discrepancy is observed during cutover or operation:
- Compare ready endpoints with load-balancer membership by zone, and record any mismatch before refreshing membership.
- Refresh service-discovery/load-balancer membership using the approved operational path.
- After the refresh, verify that traffic distribution by zone has returned to the established baseline.
- Confirm queue occupancy remains at baseline and caller error rates remain at baseline.
- Before closure, reconcile every accepted request to exactly one caller-visible terminal result. Confirm there is no duplicated accepted work, no unaccounted accepted work, and no leaked queue occupancy.
- Do not close the check if any membership mismatch persists, traffic distribution has not returned to baseline, queue occupancy or caller errors are above baseline, or request reconciliation is incomplete; investigate and escalate through the existing ingest-edge path.

This bounded check does not change the owner map and does not make Alex the routine operator. It adds a validation and reconciliation check only; existing ownership, operation, escalation, and rollback boundaries remain unchanged.

## Tenant-burst operating check — 2027-09-02

During a tenant-burst exercise or cutover observation:
- Allow at most eight waiting requests for any one tenant.
- Excess requests must remain retryable and fail before acceptance; they must not enter accepted work or be counted as accepted requests.
- Reconcile every accepted request to exactly one terminal result, with no duplicate or unaccounted accepted work.
- Confirm other tenants remain at their established baseline and caller-error behavior remains at baseline.
- After the queue is emptied, verify that queue occupancy ends at zero.
- Do not close the check if the per-tenant waiting limit, retryable pre-acceptance behavior, one-terminal-result reconciliation, other-tenant baseline, caller-error baseline, or zero-at-empty-queue condition is not met; investigate and escalate through the existing ingest-edge path.

This tenant-burst operating check does not transfer implementation, release, or rollback ownership from Yuki’s mapped path. It adds an operating validation only; the existing owner map and ownership boundaries remain unchanged.

arguments.body:
# Cross-service failure-case intake template

## Current intake rule

A cross-service exception enters review only when all four parts are present:

1. Affected component: name the component involved.
2. Mapped owner: name the implementation or release owner mapped to that component.
3. Selected boundary: choose exactly one boundary from `invariant`, `provenance`, `failure_mode`, `ownership`, or `escalation`.
4. Observed condition: state a concrete observed failed or at-risk condition; do not submit only “needs review,” “possible risk,” or another unsupported concern.

Nadia owns the front-door triage lane for asynchronous cross-service exceptions. If any part is missing or vague, she returns the request to the mapped owner without review. A complete request routes to the owner for its one selected boundary; Alex receives it only when that boundary needs his review. Nadia does not make implementation, release, or rollback decisions.

## Intake record

- Affected component:
- Mapped implementation or release owner:
- Selected boundary (exactly one): `invariant` | `provenance` | `failure_mode` | `ownership` | `escalation`
- Concrete observed failed or at-risk condition:
- Evidence and links:
- Requested review question:

## Ownership and decision boundary

The mapped implementation or release owner remains responsible for ordinary implementation and release decisions. This intake rule routes review; it does not create a new approval gate, program-owner role, or release authority for Alex. Rollback execution and operational decisions remain with the mapped service owner and established incident process. Nadia triages and routes only; she does not decide implementation, release, or rollback. Wes teaches the responder path, Nadia reviews postmortem material, and Alex maintains only the cross-service failure cases and reviews a selected boundary when routed to him.

## Facilitator use

Use one selected boundary per case. Keep the observed condition concrete and distinguish evidence from a request for review. For responder exercises, preserve the separation between routing/serving eligibility and terminal request accounting; a restart is not acceptance evidence, and replay samples are not live rollback criteria. Keep training cases bounded: they do not by themselves establish a production change, release approval, rollback decision, or ownership change.

## Historical scenarios

All historical scenarios below this template are retained unchanged.

## Historical scenarios

### Lantern migration preflight — April 27, 2026

In staging, all 20 unauthorized lookups were ultimately denied, but every one constructed and initialized the incident-load adapter before authorization completed; 2 of those 20 also accessed the source. Treat this as a blocked pre-authorization candidate, not a deployed customer incident. Customer access remained unchanged while the candidate stayed undeployed. arguments.title: ingest-edge: cutover playbook
arguments.body:
ingest-edge cutover playbook

Scope
- This runbook covers the current ingest-edge deployment and production cutover flow.
- legacy-aggregator is not part of the ingest-edge path. Do not use its routing, validation, or incident-response steps here.

1. Prepare
- Confirm the ingest-edge version and deployment configuration are ready for release.
- Review dashboards and alert coverage for ingest-edge before the cutover.
- Schedule staging cutovers for Monday morning; reserve Friday afternoons for review and preparation rather than deployment.

2. Validate in staging
- Deploy the candidate ingest-edge version to staging.
- Exercise the ingest-edge flow and confirm events are processed successfully.
- Check ingest-edge latency, error rate, throughput, and dropped-event signals before proceeding.

3. Cut over production
- Deploy the validated version to production during the approved window.
- Monitor ingest-edge dashboards and alerts continuously for the first 90 minutes.
- Confirm there are no event drops and that latency and error rates remain at their expected baseline.

4. Complete the observation check
- For the v2.19.4 cutover, continue monitoring through the formal 48-hour production check, due April 4, 2024.
- Confirm there are no dropped events, latency or error-rate regressions, or Prometheus anomalies.
- If the checks are clean, mark the cutover complete and file the close-out note.

5. Incident handling
- For an ingest-edge issue, use the ingest-edge dashboards, alerts, logs, and escalation path. Do not fall back to legacy-aggregator procedures.
- Record the observed impact, affected version, timeline, and mitigation in the cutover close-out or incident record.

Service note — OTel collector 0.91 rollout (2023-07-27)
- Production-clean after the heightened watch: error rate and CPU stayed flat.
- p95 memory settled about 5% above the pre-bump collector baseline, still within normal headroom.
- Future collector bumps still require staging replay plus an explicit memory watch.

Service note — OTel exporter retry-only change (sha:0a91b7c)
- This note covers the exporter retry change only; it is not a collector-wide tuning guide.
- Exporter retry max_interval is 15 seconds.
- Exporter retry max_elapsed_time is 5 minutes.
- Memory-limiter settings were deliberately not part of this patch.
- After deployment, check dropped writes, backpressure counters, and retry log volume.

## OTel exporter retry-only change — Oct 2023 note

For the retry-only OTel collector change deployed as `sha:0a91b7c`, the operational intent was to reduce staging/prod exporter retry noise without hiding real pressure signals.

Settings in scope:
- `max_interval`: 15 seconds
- `max_elapsed_time`: 5 minutes

Settings explicitly out of scope:
- Memory-limiter settings were not changed in this patch.

Post-deploy checks:
- Dropped writes should stay at zero.
- Backpressure counters should remain visible.
- Exporter retry log volume should decrease, but not by suppressing real backpressure evidence.

If dropped writes appear or backpressure counters disappear, treat that as a signal problem rather than a successful noise reduction.

## Staging-drill hygiene — 2024-01-03 after-action

Before opening the deploy-pipeline staging lane for an ingest-edge rollback drill:
- Verify the load-test tag TTL.
- Confirm the cleanup owner for the load-test tag and related staging artifacts.
- Do not open the staging lane until both the TTL and cleanup owner are explicitly verified.

Dec 22 boundaries:
- This guidance applies to the deploy-pipeline path only.
- Wes can perform the daylight first pass for this staging-drill class.
- Escalate unsafe or ambiguous signals rather than proceeding on assumption.
- This does not change production ownership or the owner map.

## Production behavior and v2.19.4 cutover record — 2024-04-02

- ingest-edge v2.19.4 is at 100% production after the full-production observation completed cleanly.
- Randomized one-to-three-second `Retry-After` behavior is now the production behavior for 429 responses; do not describe it as canary-only or restore the baseline behavior solely because the observation completed.
- The formal 48-hour production check remains due April 4, 2024.
- Synchronized retry bursts did not reform after 429 responses during the 50% gate.

Explicit stop boundaries for this cutover
Immediately stop the rollout, hold further promotion, and prepare rollback if any one of the following occurs:
- Any increase in 5xx responses.
- p99 latency at or above 190 ms.
- Queue depth at or above 76%.
- Accepted-throughput loss at or above 3% versus baseline.
- Retry volume at or above 130,000 attempts per second.

Observed gate maxima
- 10% gate: peak retries 123,000 attempts per second; p99 172 ms; queue depth 74%; accepted throughput 2.4% below baseline; no 5xx increase.
- 50% gate: peak retries 128,000 attempts per second; p99 186 ms; queue depth 75%; accepted throughput 2.8% below baseline; no 5xx increase.
- 100% gate/full-production observation: peak retries 129,000 attempts per second; p99 188 ms; queue depth 75%; accepted throughput 2.9% below baseline; no 5xx increase.

All production gates passed. Keep v2.19.4 at 100% and retain the randomized one-to-three-second `Retry-After` behavior as production behavior. The explicit stop boundaries remain in force through the formal 48-hour check.

## Production tenant-fair queue behavior — 2024-07-05

The mapped owner completed the remaining ingest-edge rollout. At both the 50% gate and full production:
- Repeated noisy-tenant tests preserved the eight-waiting cap per tenant.
- Newly queued low-volume tenants entered the ring immediately.
- Work-conserving dispatch used each eligible slot.
- Empty tenants were removed from the ring after cancellation.
- Every queue-cap response retained `Retry-After`.
- Existing active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, and restart checks remained clean.

Preserve these existing ingest-edge requirements during cutover, operation, and rollback:
- No more than four active work items per pod.
- No more than two active work items per tenant.
- Bounded decompression must remain enforced.
- Retry behavior and its existing requirements must remain enforced, including retaining `Retry-After` on queue-cap responses.

Treat any loss of the eight-waiting cap, delayed ring admission for newly queued low-volume tenants, unused eligible dispatch capacity, failure to remove empty tenants after cancellation, missing `Retry-After`, or regression in active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, or restart checks as a rollout/operational signal requiring investigation before further promotion.

## Bounded service-discovery membership check — May 24 zone imbalance

Use this bounded check when a zone imbalance or similar service-discovery membership discrepancy is observed during cutover or operation:
- Compare ready endpoints with load-balancer membership by zone, and record any mismatch before refreshing membership.
- Refresh service-discovery/load-balancer membership using the approved operational path.
- After the refresh, verify that traffic distribution by zone has returned to the established baseline.
- Confirm queue occupancy remains at baseline and caller error rates remain at baseline.
- Before closure, reconcile every accepted request to exactly one caller-visible terminal result. Confirm there is no duplicated accepted work, no unaccounted accepted work, and no leaked queue occupancy.
- Do not close the check if any membership mismatch persists, traffic distribution has not returned to baseline, queue occupancy or caller errors are above baseline, or request reconciliation is incomplete; investigate and escalate through the existing ingest-edge path.

This bounded check does not change the owner map and does not make Alex the routine operator. It adds a validation and reconciliation check only; existing ownership, operation, escalation, and rollback boundaries remain unchanged.

messages.content:
Privileged-access recertification checklist — due May 21

For each grant in ingest-edge, shard-keeper, legacy-aggregator, and every read-only system:

1. Current primary-owner access
   - Is the repository/service still part of my current role?
   - Do I currently own an approved operational responsibility?
   - Is the permission level no broader than needed for implementation, release, rollback, or operations?
   - Retain only the minimum required grant; document the specific duty it supports.
   - Do not treat access as evidence that I own the service.

2. Backup or exception access
   - Is there a named current primary owner?
   - Is my backup/fallback responsibility explicitly documented and still active?
   - Is the exception approved, bounded, and time-limited?
   - Confirm the trigger, scope, expiration/review date, and approving authority.
   - Retain only if I could realistically be called on to perform that backup duty.

3. Stale migration-era access
   - Was the grant inherited from a migration, former ownership assignment, temporary incident, or old team?
   - Is the former responsibility no longer part of my role?
   - Is there no current approver, expiry, named fallback duty, or operational need?
   - Remove it, especially unused write, deploy, admin, or credential-management access.
   - For read-only access, retain only a documented present-day need; “useful to have” is not sufficient.

Final attestation checks

   - Separate repository access from operational access.
   - Verify each retained grant against the current role, not historical ownership.
   - Record exceptions and unknowns rather than inferring continued need.
   - Certify only the grants personally inspected and still required.
   - Remember: this review changes access certification, not service ownership.

arguments.title: metrics-router: service identity and ownership
arguments.body:
# Service identity and ownership

Effective 2025-12-05:
- Primary owner: Wes.
- Backup: Alex.
- Wes owns routine metrics-router implementation, production operations, release and rollback decisions, and decisions to open owner-led windows under the existing deploy-pipeline, canary, health-return, stop, and rollback rules.
- Alex is the architectural reviewer and escalation path when a cross-service invariant, provenance issue, or failure-mode exception is triggered. Alex may make a fresh opening decision while covering for an unavailable Wes, but does not gate ordinary metrics-router windows.

Boundaries preserved:
- The accepted-batch diagnostic is qualified for prospective production observation only. It does not retroactively establish whether any accepted batch was lost on October 6.
- The broader Mosaic scale-response cycle remains open. No capacity-related production window is open or authorized.
- Infra on-call roster is unchanged.
- Ingest-edge and shard-keeper ownership are unchanged. Shard-keeper remains outside Wes's solo scope unless Alex or the Cyrus-team backup explicitly pairs with him.
- Existing deploy-pipeline, canary, health-return, stop, rollback, provenance, and failure-mode rules remain in force.

1. Check the OTel collector batch window. 2. Compare p99 vs baseline. 3. Roll back via pipeline if regression confirmed. 4. If a cardinality alert coincides with scheduled load-test traffic, inspect the label set (especially `experiment_id`) and confirm the traffic source before treating it as a service regression; coordinate with the load-test owner and stop the test if appropriate. This note does not change service ownership.

Generation and cleanup checks:
- Compare p99 by pod with active-generation counts, retired-generation counts, and stop-the-world cleanup pause durations. Capture generation counts and heap evidence for the canary record.
- Verify active-generation consistency across pods, route parity, dropped series, reload failures, and restarts.
- Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or if cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds; investigate and drain or clean up before resuming pushes.
- Do not roll back solely because a transient p99 spike recovered. Preserve rollback when active-generation inconsistency, route-delivery divergence, or dropped series is observed; also roll back when the defined regression signals worsen or spread.

Owner-led-window rule:
- Each configuration window is opened by the metrics-router primary under the existing deploy-pipeline, canary, health-return, stop, and rollback rules; it is an opening decision for the window, not per-push approval.
- The primary may make a fresh opening decision after verifying opening health. Alex may make that decision while covering for an unavailable Wes.
- Mapped operators may make single-file pushes while retired generations remain at four or fewer, cleanup pauses remain at or below 100 milliseconds, and the full health set returns to baseline after every push.
- Exceeding either threshold stops the window immediately.
- After recovery, a fresh decision permits exactly one fully observed push. Another window requires a separate fresh decision after that push returns the full health set to baseline.
- Consistency, parity, dropped-series, reload, restart, and defined regression failures remain rollback conditions.

Dated 2025-12-05 — Ownership decision:
- Wes is metrics-router primary; Alex is backup.
- Wes owns routine implementation, production operations, release and rollback decisions, and ordinary owner-led-window opening decisions under the rules above.
- Alex remains architectural reviewer and escalation path only for cross-service invariant, provenance, or failure-mode exceptions, and may cover ordinary opening decisions when Wes is unavailable.
- This ownership change does not authorize a capacity-related production window, change the qualified status of the accepted-batch diagnostic, or change ingest-edge, Infra on-call, or shard-keeper ownership. Shard-keeper remains outside Wes's solo scope unless Alex or the Cyrus-team backup explicitly pairs with him.

# metrics-router on-call handoff checklist

Ownership effective 2025-12-05:
- Primary: Wes.
- Backup: Alex.
- Wes owns routine metrics-router implementation, production operations, release and rollback decisions, and ordinary owner-led-window opening decisions under the existing deploy-pipeline, canary, health-return, stop, and rollback rules.
- Alex is the architectural reviewer and escalation path for cross-service invariant, provenance, or failure-mode exceptions. Alex may cover ordinary opening decisions when Wes is unavailable.

At handoff, record:
- Active deploys and rollback state.
- Open incidents and current mitigations.
- Recent canary state, including p99, error rate, dropped writes, rollup-service lag, active/retired generations, cleanup pauses, route parity, reloads, restarts, and return-to-baseline evidence.
- Any open owner-led window and its opening decision, observed pushes, stop conditions, and closure state.
- Accepted-batch diagnostic status: qualified for prospective production observation only; it does not establish retrospectively whether any accepted batch was lost on October 6.
- Mosaic scale-response status: broader cycle remains open; no capacity-related production window is open or authorized.
- Current Infra on-call roster, which is unchanged.

Scope boundaries:
- Ingest-edge ownership is unchanged.
- Shard-keeper ownership is unchanged and remains outside Wes's solo scope unless Alex or the Cyrus-team backup explicitly pairs with him.
- Escalate to Alex when a cross-service invariant, provenance issue, or failure-mode exception is triggered; do not use escalation as a gate for ordinary metrics-router windows.

Decision recorded 2025-12-05 after review with Hema, Wes, and Alex:
- Wes is metrics-router primary and Alex is backup, effective today.
- Wes owns routine metrics-router implementation, production operations, release and rollback decisions, and ordinary owner-led-window opening decisions under the existing deploy-pipeline, canary, health-return, stop, and rollback rules.
- Alex remains the architectural reviewer and escalation path for cross-service invariant, provenance, or failure-mode exceptions, and may cover an opening decision while Wes is unavailable; Alex does not gate ordinary metrics-router windows.

Preserved boundaries:
- The accepted-batch diagnostic is qualified for prospective production observation only and does not retroactively establish whether any accepted batch was lost on October 6.
- The broader Mosaic scale-response cycle remains open; no capacity-related production window is open or authorized.
- Infra on-call roster unchanged; ingest-edge and shard-keeper ownership unchanged.
- Shard-keeper remains outside Wes's solo scope unless Alex or the Cyrus-team backup explicitly pairs with him.

ingest-edge cutover playbook

Scope
- This runbook covers the current ingest-edge deployment and production cutover flow.
- legacy-aggregator is not part of the ingest-edge path. Do not use its routing, validation, or incident-response steps here.

1. Prepare
- Confirm the ingest-edge version and deployment configuration are ready for release.
- Review dashboards and alert coverage for ingest-edge before the cutover.
- Schedule staging cutovers for Monday morning; reserve Friday afternoons for review and preparation rather than deployment.

2. Validate in staging
- Deploy the candidate ingest-edge version to staging.
- Exercise the ingest-edge flow and confirm events are processed successfully.
- Check ingest-edge latency, error rate, throughput, and dropped-event signals before proceeding.

3. Cut over production
- Deploy the validated version to production during the approved window.
- Monitor ingest-edge dashboards and alerts continuously for the first 90 minutes.
- Confirm there are no event drops and that latency and error rates remain at their expected baseline.

4. Complete the observation check
- For the v2.19.4 cutover, continue monitoring through the formal 48-hour production check, due April 4, 2024.
- Confirm there are no dropped events, latency or error-rate regressions, or Prometheus anomalies.
- If the checks are clean, mark the cutover complete and file the close-out note.

5. Incident handling
- For an ingest-edge issue, use the ingest-edge dashboards, alerts, logs, and escalation path. Do not fall back to legacy-aggregator procedures.
- Record the observed impact, affected version, timeline, and mitigation in the cutover close-out or incident record.

- p95 memory settled about 5% above the pre-bump collector baseline, still within normal headroom.
- Future collector bumps still require staging replay plus an explicit memory watch.

Service note — OTel exporter retry-only change (sha:0a91b7c)
- This note covers the exporter retry change only; it is not a collector-wide tuning guide.
- Exporter retry max_interval is 15 seconds.
- Exporter retry max_elapsed_time is 5 minutes.
- Memory-limiter settings were deliberately not part of this patch.
- After deployment, check dropped writes, backpressure counters, and retry log volume.

OTel exporter retry-only change — Oct 2023 note

For the retry-only OTel collector change deployed as sha:0a91b7c, the operational intent was to reduce staging/prod exporter retry noise without hiding real pressure signals.

Settings in scope:
- max_interval: 15 seconds
- max_elapsed_time: 5 minutes

Settings explicitly out of scope:
- Memory-limiter settings were not changed in this patch.

Post-deploy checks:
- Dropped writes should stay at zero.
- Backpressure counters should remain visible.
- Exporter retry log volume should decrease, but not by suppressing real backpressure evidence.

If dropped writes appear or backpressure counters disappear, treat that as a signal problem rather than a successful noise reduction.

Alex 2027 self-review — working draft

Outcomes and impact

I strengthened delivery by making cross-service contracts and failure modes explicit while keeping execution with mapped owners. My bounded failure-condition review of Yuki’s owner-held ingest-edge decoder release covered a request-wide 1,048,576-byte decoded-attribute limit across all gzip members and a 72-request decode-admission cap. The separate 8,000-point whole-batch rule and eight-waiting-requests-per-tenant limit remained in force; production observation closed with no rollback. I completed bounded contract, provenance, invariant, and failure-mode work for Lantern and related systems. Lantern activated cleanly, but Lantern’s October 1–December 15 package remains open pending reconciliation and zero unresolved rows before freeze. The named triggered reviews—metrics-router cancellation terminal-accounting and rollup-service tenant-identity—also remain open. Hema accepted my Q4 intake objectives without revision: the readout will cover routed and returned requests and return reasons, with Nadia retaining front-door triage. My work is triggered boundary review; mapped owners retain implementation, release, and rollback authority.

How I worked

I worked from bounded evidence: naming the invariant, source, owner, failure condition, and closure evidence. I separated my triggered boundary reviews from mapped-owner implementation, release, and rollback authority, and escalated only when a boundary was triggered. I kept Nadia’s front-door triage role and preserved ownership clarity with Yuki, Wes, Roman, and Product Engineering. I treated clean results as bounded claims, kept open evidence visible, and documented what remained unresolved rather than turning partial validation into closure. Reusable review records and explicit provenance helped owners act without duplicated responsibility.

Growth focus for 2028

Build reusable evidence and contract patterns for cancellation, disconnect, crash recovery, tenant identity, and provenance boundaries. Improve early intake signal quality while keeping Nadia’s triage role and mapped owners’ implementation, release, and rollback authority intact. Close the metrics-router and rollup-service reviews through executable evidence, not assumption, and make the evidence easier for owners to consume without creating a new approval gate.

arguments.body:
ingest-edge cutover playbook

Scope
- This runbook covers the current ingest-edge deployment and production cutover flow.
- legacy-aggregator is not part of the ingest-edge path. Do not use its routing, validation, or incident-response steps here.

1. Prepare
- Confirm the ingest-edge version and deployment configuration are ready for release.
- Review dashboards and alert coverage for ingest-edge before the cutover.
- Schedule staging cutovers for Monday morning; reserve Friday afternoons for review and preparation rather than deployment.

2. Validate in staging
- Deploy the candidate ingest-edge version to staging.
- Exercise the ingest-edge flow and confirm events are processed successfully.
- Check ingest-edge latency, error rate, throughput, and dropped-event signals before proceeding.

3. Cut over production
- Deploy the validated version to production during the approved window.
- Monitor ingest-edge dashboards and alerts continuously for the first 90 minutes.
- Confirm there are no event drops and that latency and error rates remain at their expected baseline.

4. Complete the observation check
- For the v2.19.4 cutover, continue monitoring through the formal 48-hour production check, due April 4, 2024.
- Confirm there are no dropped events, latency or error-rate regressions, or Prometheus anomalies.
- If the checks are clean, mark the cutover complete and file the close-out note.

5. Incident handling
- For an ingest-edge issue, use the ingest-edge dashboards, alerts, logs, and escalation path. Do not fall back to legacy-aggregator procedures.
- Record the observed impact, affected version, timeline, and mitigation in the cutover close-out or incident record.

Service note — OTel collector 0.91 rollout (2023-07-27)
- Production-clean after the heightened watch: error rate and CPU stayed flat.
- p95 memory settled about 5% above the pre-bump collector baseline, still within normal headroom.
- Future collector bumps still require staging replay plus an explicit memory watch.

Service note — OTel exporter retry-only change (sha:0a91b7c)
- This note covers the exporter retry change only; it is not a collector-wide tuning guide.
- Exporter retry max_interval is 15 seconds.
- Exporter retry max_elapsed_time is 5 minutes.
- Memory-limiter settings were deliberately not part of this patch.
- After deployment, check dropped writes, backpressure counters, and retry log volume.

## OTel exporter retry-only change — Oct 2023 note

For the retry-only OTel collector change deployed as `sha:0a91b7c`, the operational intent was to reduce staging/prod exporter retry noise without hiding real pressure signals.

Settings in scope:
- `max_interval`: 15 seconds
- `max_elapsed_time`: 5 minutes

Settings explicitly out of scope:
- Memory-limiter settings were not changed in this patch.

Post-deploy checks:
- Dropped writes should stay at zero.
- Backpressure counters should remain visible.
- Exporter retry log volume should decrease, but not by suppressing real backpressure evidence.

If dropped writes appear or backpressure counters disappear, treat that as a signal problem rather than a successful noise reduction.

## Staging-drill hygiene — 2024-01-03 after-action

Before opening the deploy-pipeline staging lane for an ingest-edge rollback drill:
- Verify the load-test tag TTL.
- Confirm the cleanup owner for the load-test tag and related staging artifacts.
- Do not open the staging lane until both the TTL and cleanup owner are explicitly verified.

Dec 22 boundaries:
- This guidance applies to the deploy-pipeline path only.
- Wes can perform the daylight first pass for this staging-drill class.
- Escalate unsafe or ambiguous signals rather than proceeding on assumption.
- This does not change production ownership or the owner map.

## Production behavior and v2.19.4 cutover record — 2024-04-02

- ingest-edge v2.19.4 is at 100% production after the full-production observation completed cleanly.
- Randomized one-to-three-second `Retry-After` behavior is now the production behavior for 429 responses; do not describe it as canary-only or restore the baseline behavior solely because the observation completed.
- The formal 48-hour production check remains due April 4, 2024.
- Synchronized retry bursts did not reform after 429 responses during the 50% gate.

Explicit stop boundaries for this cutover
Immediately stop the rollout, hold further promotion, and prepare rollback if any one of the following occurs:
- Any increase in 5xx responses.
- p99 latency at or above 190 ms.
- Queue depth at or above 76%.
- Accepted-throughput loss at or above 3% versus baseline.
- Retry volume at or above 130,000 attempts per second.

Observed gate maxima
- 10% gate: peak retries 123,000 attempts per second; p99 172 ms; queue depth 74%; accepted throughput 2.4% below baseline; no 5xx increase.
- 50% gate: peak retries 128,000 attempts per second; p99 186 ms; queue depth 75%; accepted throughput 2.8% below baseline; no 5xx increase.
- 100% gate/full-production observation: peak retries 129,000 attempts per second; p99 188 ms; queue depth 75%; accepted throughput 2.9% below baseline; no 5xx increase.

All production gates passed. Keep v2.19.4 at 100% and retain the randomized one-to-three-second `Retry-After` behavior as production behavior. The explicit stop boundaries remain in force through the formal 48-hour check.

## Production tenant-fair queue behavior — 2024-07-05

The mapped owner completed the remaining ingest-edge rollout. At both the 50% gate and full production:
- Repeated noisy-tenant tests preserved the eight-waiting cap per tenant.
- Newly queued low-volume tenants entered the ring immediately.
- Work-conserving dispatch used each eligible slot.
- Empty tenants were removed from the ring after cancellation.
- Every queue-cap response retained `Retry-After`.
- Existing active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, and restart checks remained clean.

Preserve these existing ingest-edge requirements during cutover, operation, and rollback:
- No more than four active work items per pod.
- No more than two active work items per tenant.
- Bounded decompression must remain enforced.
- Retry behavior and its existing requirements must remain enforced, including retaining `Retry-After` on queue-cap responses.

Treat any loss of the eight-waiting cap, delayed ring admission for newly queued low-volume tenants, unused eligible dispatch capacity, failure to remove empty tenants after cancellation, missing `Retry-After`, or regression in active-work, accepted-point, dropped-point, or restart checks as a rollout/operational signal requiring investigation before further promotion.

## Bounded service-discovery membership check — May 24 zone imbalance

Use this bounded check when a zone imbalance or similar service-discovery membership discrepancy is observed during cutover or operation:
- Compare ready endpoints with load-balancer membership by zone, and record any mismatch before refreshing membership.
- Refresh service-discovery/load-balancer membership using the approved operational path.
- After the refresh, verify that traffic distribution by zone has returned to the established baseline.
- Confirm queue occupancy remains at baseline and caller error rates remain at baseline.
- Before closure, reconcile every accepted request to exactly one caller-visible terminal result. Confirm there is no duplicated accepted work, no unaccounted accepted work, and no leaked queue occupancy.
- Do not close the check if any membership mismatch persists, traffic distribution has not returned to baseline, queue occupancy or caller errors are above baseline, or request reconciliation is incomplete; investigate and escalate through the existing ingest-edge path.

This bounded check does not change the owner map and does not make Alex the routine operator. It adds a validation and reconciliation check only; existing ownership, operation, escalation, and rollback boundaries remain unchanged.

## Tenant-burst operating check — 2027-09-02

During a tenant-burst exercise or cutover observation:
- Allow at most eight waiting requests for any one tenant.
- Excess requests must remain retryable and fail before acceptance; they must not enter accepted work or be counted as accepted requests.
- Reconcile every accepted request to exactly one terminal result, with no duplicate or unaccounted accepted work.
- Confirm other tenants remain at their established baseline and caller-error behavior remains at baseline.
- After the queue is emptied, verify that queue occupancy ends at zero.
- Do not close the check if the per-tenant waiting limit, retryable pre-acceptance behavior, one-terminal-result reconciliation, other-tenant baseline, caller-error baseline, or zero-at-empty-queue condition is not met; investigate and escalate through the existing ingest-edge path.

This tenant-burst operating check does not transfer implementation, release, or rollback ownership from Yuki’s mapped path. It adds an operating validation only; the existing owner map and ownership boundaries remain unchanged.
